Three of the hikers and two dogs were caught in the avalanche with one hiker and the two dogs buried. Two others were partially buried. Rescue efforts were unsuccessful with one hiker killed, along with the two dogs. The partially buried hikers survived with minor injuries.

Rapid snowmelt from the Dolores River led to various drainages breaching their banks. This resulted in flooded downtown residential buildings in the town of Dolores. The water also flooded streets, some yards, and school playgrounds. Flood waters did not recede for several days.

The Pagosa Ranger District in the San Juan National Forest reported at least three instances of flooding on Piedra Road (CR 600) north of the Turkey Springs Trailhead. The flooding was the result of rapid runoff from snowmelt.

Rapid snowmelt resulted in Dry Creek, which runs underneath Highway 40, coming out of its banks. As a result, Highway 40 was closed and shut down in both directions from Craig to Steamboat Springs due to safety concerns. Schools in Hayden were closed. Flood waters did not recede for several days.

Rapid snowmelt resulted in flooding across portions of Moffat County, focused in downtown Craig. Fortification Creek near City Park exceeded its banks. Several county roads were closed as a result of the flooding. Flood waters did not recede for a couple of days.
Rapid snowmelt resulted in flooding across Bell Creek Road outside Paonia as Bell Creek overran its banks.

Rapid snowmelt resulted in flooding across Road 9.7 in Dolores County, as the Dolores River overran its banks. The road was closed for a prolonged period as flood waters did not recede for several days. The accelerated snowmelt and subsequent pooling of water flooded the local high school, which damaged the gym flooring.
As a result of rapid snowmelt, a portion of Spring Canyon Road in Montrose County was closed due to flooding.
Rapid snowmelt led the Dolores River to overrun its banks. This led to flooding across Y11 Road in Montrose County, near Uravan.
Rapid snowmelt resulted in portions of Dave Wood Road to be washed out from flooding.

The Piedra River overran its banks due to rapid snowmelt. This led to portions of Colorado Highway 151, south of Chimney Rock National Monument, to be flooded and closed for an extended period of time.
A peak wind gust of 69 MPH was measured by the automated weather station at the Meeker Coulter Field Airport with a peak gust of 62 mph occurring at the Craig-Moffat Airport.
A peak wind gust of 79 MPH was measured by the automated weather station at Douglas Pass.

A fire of unknown origins started about 1.2 miles east of Carbondale along County Road 100.  Wind gusts to 50 mph quickly spread the fire to over 1000 acres, and the fire jumped across the Roaring Fork River in the process. Four houses caught on fire, though efforts by firefighters prevented the houses from being destroyed. Many lawns and trees were charred.  A man received burns to the back of his head and arms as he was fishing along the Roaring Fork River.  County Road 100 was closed for an extensive period of time, while Highway 82 was closed for three hours.  Hundreds of residents and a large number of livestock in the area were evacuated.  There were 140 firefighters who fought the blaze, along with nearly as many volunteers.

Rapid snowmelt resulted in Dry Creek, which runs underneath S Popular Street, coming out of its banks. As a result, S Popular Street near Harvest Drive was closed due to flooding. Flood waters did not recede for several days.
Overnight lows ranged from 25 to 29 degrees across the area, including a low of 28 degrees at the Grand Junction Regional Airport.

The Red Bridge Fire started Sunday evening south of Fort Duchesne and burned nearly 460 acres of federal land. It was fully contained by Wednesday evening. Investigators determined the fire was human caused.

Saturated soils from excessive runoff of melting snow lead to numerous mud and debris flows near Glenwood Springs, CO and the near the Hanging Lake Trail in Glenwood Canyon. The mud trapped a train traveling through the west side of Glenwood Springs with no injuries reported. Access to the Hanging Lake Trail was cutoff with roadway closures. Mud also slid off of Red Mountain south of Glenwood Springs, prompting the additional closures of some roadways and a private bridge was washed out.

Excessive spring runoff and debris backing up in culverts led to a large sinkhole developing on Highway 133 north of Paonia and south of Somerset, Colorado between mile markers 14 and 19. This resulted in the closure of the highway to allow emergency repairs to be made. The sinking soils were first noticed on April 29, 2023 with the eventual collapse of the highway occurring on May 2, 2023.
Montrose County Government Facebook post reported the X4 Road to the Cashin Cooper Mine was closed due to flooding from increased snowmelt.
Warm temperatures increased snowmelt and caused flooding on Routt County Road 44 between Highway 40 and Routt County Road 42. The road was closed for an extended period of time.
Nickel-size hail pummeled the oil and gas fields in west-central Uintah County.
A culvert failed due to excess runoff along Colorado Highway 133 in Bear Creek, or near mile marker 16.
Increased flood waters due to rapid snowmelt damaged a private bridge off of Colorado Highway 145, near mile marker 22.
A large mudslide occurred as a result of rapid snowmelt on County Road 129 south of Clark near Fetcher Ranch.

West Creek in Mesa County ran high and fast as a result of accelerated snowmelt resulting in the creek with flooding observed by local law enforcement. West Creek drains south into the Dolores River. A 94-year old man drowned after accidentally backing his ATV into West Creek and was swept downstream.
Warm temperatures increased snowmelt and caused flooding at the Oxbow Preserve along the Animas River, which led to its closure.
Warm temperatures increased snowmelt and caused flooding on the lower Prince Creek trails, which ran along Prince Creek. High water submerged bridges and led to damage on the trails.
Warm temperatures increased snowmelt and caused a debris flow on unsettled slopes on the Rio Grande Trail in Snowmass Canyon. The trail ran along the Roaring Fork River.
Warm temperatures increased snowmelt and caused flooding on the low-lying Stocks Drive near Utah Highway 191.
Warm temperatures increased snowmelt and caused flooding on the low-lying Sunny Acres Lane, which sits near Pack Creek, near Utah Highway 191.
Increased flood waters due to rapid snowmelt led to water and debris across Fall Creek Road from County Road 56L to the Little Cone Ranch Subdivision. The road was closed for several hours.
Generally 6 to 9 inches of snow fell at elevations above 9500 feet. A trained spotter reported a locally higher amount of 11 inches near Trout Lake.

Part of the Riverfront Trail was closed for several days in Grand Junction as a result of flooding due to accelerated snowmelt. The trail at the Redlands Parkway underpass was under water, but the main road itself remained dry.
Increased snowmelt along the Green River resulted in flooding on portions of Mineral Bottom Road.

Increased snowmelt along the Dolores River led to the inundation of the campground and parking lot along the boat launch at the Bradfield Recreation Site outside Cahone. Some vehicles were stuck in the mud as a result.

Closures were implemented on the outer lane of I-70 at Skipper Island west of Fruita in both directions as a result of flooding along the Colorado River. The closure was updated to only include the right lane of I-70 westbound several days later.
An NWS employee riding on a bike trail outside Loma reported flooding along the trail near Reed Wash. The river was running incredibly high underneath the I-70 bridge.
County Road 2 next to the USGS's Slater Fork gage south of the Wyoming/Colorado border had one lane closed due to flooding along Slater Creek.
The boat ramp at Bedrock along the Dolores River was inaccessible due to flooding on the river.
Seedhouse Road in Routt County northeast of Clark was closed between mile markers 3 and 5 as a result of flooding.
Flooding occurred at the Gypsum Valley Boat Launch as a result of increased snowmelt and flow along the Dolores River.
Flooding along the Yampa River resulted in the closure of the Deerlodge Park Campground within Dinosaur National Monument.

Snowmelt produced a washout on National Forest System Road (NFSR) #525-Potter Basin road located at mile post 1.172 on the Ouray Ranger District, northeast of 25 Mesa Guard Station. The road was not passable and remained closed.

The Bureau of Land Management reported high flows along the Colorado River near Moab. This led to flooding at the takeout boat ramp near Moab as well as in several campgrounds along the river. This included the King's Bottom, Williams Bottom, Jaycee Park, Hal Canyon, Goose Island, Gold Bar campgrounds as well as the lower section of Drinks Canyon Campground.

The Colorado River in Glenwood Canyon ran high and fast as a result of accelerated snowmelt. While rafting in Glenwood Canyon, two rafters fell into the river while navigating a rapid and eddy. Both men were pulled from the water and brought back to shore. The rafting party began CPR on the two individuals - one rafter responded, but the other one did not.
Hail estimated to be one inch in diameter fell near Rangely.
Flooding on Surface Creek led to the closure of a recreational trail along the river, near Cedaredge, as the trail was washed out.

Increased snowmelt along the Colorado River led to the closure of Hanging Lake Trail near Glenwood Springs. Water flowed directly down parts of the trail, forcing the closure for approximately a week or so.
Flooding occurred at Anders Ranch along East River as a result of increased flows from snowmelt.

Emergency management reported flooding along portions of the North Fork of the Gunnison River near Hotchkiss, mainly in the form of significant erosion of banks along the river. A few cars from a junkyard that was located right against the river bank were taken by the water.
Snowfall of 6 to 10 inches occurred. Wind gusts of 25 to 40 mph produced blowing and drifting snow.

Numerous natural and human caused avalanches occurred. The Iron Horse Bicycle Classic road race and tour was cancelled due to the snow. This was the first time in its 37 year history that the Durango to Silverton race was cancelled.

Accelerated snowmelt from a near-record snowpack due to above normal temperatures produced high and fast flow on the North Fork of the Gunnison River near Paonia, Colorado. This led to a power pole that was near the river to be washed out, resulting in a power outage for almost 700 people between Paonia and Hotchkiss.

Kebler Pass sustained major damage due to excessive runoff, knocking out a significant portion of the road about halfway through the pass. Due to the road not being passable by vehicle, the pass will remain closed until repairs can be made and the road is rebuilt. There is no estimated time on when Kebler Pass will reopen.
Accelerated snowmelt led to high rises in Roubideau Creek which subsequently led to the washout of portions of Roubideau Canyon Road which runs along the creek.

Snowmelt produced a washout on National Forest System Road (NFSR) #709-Coal Creek road located at mile post 2 in the Paonia Ranger District. The road was not passable and remained closed.

The Roaring Fork River ran high and fast as a result of accelerated snowmelt. Rescuers were unable to resuscitate a person they recovered from the river near the Lazy Glen subdivision after strong, runoff-fueled currents carried the victim downstream roughly 1 1/2 to 2 miles. It did not appear the person had been in a water vessel like a boat or raft. The incident had the makings of someone falling into the river from its banks, but that wasn���t a certainty. Age and gender of victim is unknown.

Accelerated snowmelt resulted in the development of a sinkhole on the edge of Brush Creek Road immediately downhill of Lower Kearns Road in Snowmass Village. The road was closed for a short while before being reopened a day or so later.

Moderate Drought conditions existed across extreme northwest Moffat County at the start of the month. Significant winter precipitation and cool spring temperatures resulted in the dissipation of drought conditions by the end of April aross northwest Moffat County.

Moderate Drought conditions diminished to a very small area of northwest Daggett County by the end of the month. For a continuation on this drought situation please see the May 2008 Storm Data publication.

Twenty-one natural avalanches on Red Mountain Pass hit the road and caused periods of road closure. Some of the avalanches were up to 8 feet deep and several hundred feet wide on the roadway.

A family rafting on the Colorado River became separated when their boat capsized due the fast and high flows as a result of recent snowmelt. First responders were able to locate all of the victims, but one minor was unresponsive to CPR.

Moderate Drought conditions continued across extreme northern Daggett County at the beginning of May. However, the combination of significant winter precipitation and cool spring weather resulted in decreased dryness and an end of the drought conditions by month's end.

Three river rafters using inflatable canoes got caught up in swift water flows which were elevated due to recent warm weather and accelerated snowmelt. One rafter got separated from the group and was discovered downstream. CPR efforts were not successful and rafter passed away.

Snowmelt runoff caused some streams and creeks to exceed bankfull resulting in minor flooding. A seasonal stream came out of its banks and flooded the basement of a home south of Crested Butte and threatened a couple other homes. Heavy equipment was used to build some dikes and divert the water. Several homes were surrounded by water near the confluence of the Slate River and East River, which is about 7 miles southeast of Crested Butte and 10 miles north of Almont. The dirt roads leading to those residences were under 3 to 6 inches of water. Additionally, the East River overflowed at a few other locations which flooded pasture land.

Snowmelt runoff caused some streams and creeks to exceed bankfull. Culverts were overwhelmed in areas and portions of roads were damaged. In some cases, minor flooding and road damage occurred due to snowmelt water that cascaded off slopes above roads. Water 6 to 8 inches deep flowed across some roads. The force of the water caused a section of road between the Elk River Guest Ranch and Vista Verde Guest Ranch to slough off. The damaged road section was about 20 feet wide and plunged 12 to 14 feet down.

The Elk River near Milner exceeded flood stage and water inundated low lying pasture and farm land adjacent to the river. The river also ran above bankfull above Clark. Reports from the Routt County emergency manager indicated some dirt roads had been covered with water.

The Elk River near Milner exceeded flood stage and inundated low lying areas adjacent to the river, mainly consisting of pasture and farm land. Flooding continued into the following month. Please see the June 2008 Storm Data publication for a continuation on this event.
This event began the last day of May and continued into June. The Elk River near Milner exceeded flood stage inundating low lying areas adjacent to the river, mainly pasture and farm land.
The East River at Almont exceeded flood stage and resulted in minor flooding of adjacent low lying areas, mainly consisting of pastureland.
The Yampa River at Deerlodge Park exceeded flood stage. The river also exceeded bankfull in the Maybell vicinity and caused flooding of a yard near the river.
The Yampa River at Deerlodge Park exceeded flood stage.

Rivers, small streams, and creeks across much of Mesa County exceeded bankfull and caused minor flooding. Emergency Manager and weather spotter reports indicated low land flooding along portions of the Colorado River from DeBeque Canyon to the Utah State Line. The Interstate 70 median east of the Loma exit was flooded. Water lapped at the side of the westbound Interstate 70 bridge near the Loma Exit causing officials to close one lane in each direction for a period. Water covered a section of the westbound interstate lanes in DeBeque Canyon and near the Highway 65 cutoff. The Colorado River was out of its banks on both sides of the river in the Highway 340 Bridge area and encroached into an adjacent State Park campground. Portions of the Colorado Riverfront Trail in Grand Junction were closed due to high water. The Gunnison River was out of its banks and covered an access road to a construction company in the vicinity of the Department of Energy.

Many trees fell across the road and stranded motorists. Some of the trees were 16 to 20 inches in diameter. No sensors nearby but wind gusts were estimated to be at least 60 mph.

Portions of a recreational bike and walking path adjacent to the Colorado River through Glenwood Canyon were flooded. Water was within a few inches of railroad tracks in the area.

One lane of westbound Interstate 70 near the Loma exit was closed for a period of time due to high water. All islands in the Colorado River were underwater. Water was within 6 to 12 inches of the bottom of four bridges that cross the river. Flows on the river peaked on June 4 and 5.

The Arkansas Loop Fire began in late June from unknown causes, 21 miles south of Durango, near Bondad. The fire grew to 127 acres before it was contained in mid July.
The Arkansas Loop Fire began in late June from unknown causes, 21 miles south of Durango, near Bondad. The fire grew to 127 acres before it was contained in mid July.

The I-70 MM217 Fire began in mid July due to a spark from a rollover accident along the interstate. The accident occurred east of Cisco near the Colorado/Utah border. It grew to 1,802 acres before being contained a couple of days later.
The Coal Mine Fire started in late June from a lightning strike, 18 miles south of Pagosa Springs, and grew to 292 acres before it was contained in mid July.
The Coal Mine Fire started in late June from a lightning strike, 18 miles south of Pagosa Springs, and grew to 292 acres before it was contained in mid July.

High temperatures of 100 to 110 degrees were reported by various automated weather stations across the Grand Valley. The Grand Junction Regional Airport set a new record high temperature for the day of 107 degrees. This also tied the all time record high for the airport. Heat indices exceeded 100 degrees during the afternoon.
The Chris Mountain Fire started in late June from a lightning strike, 12 miles west of Pagosa Springs, and grew to 511 acres before it was contained in late July.

A peak wind gust of 59 MPH was measured by the automated weather station at Asphalt Ridge, 3 miles southwest of Vernal.
The Howard Fire started in mid July from a lightning strike near Meeker, and grew to 255 acres before it was contained at the end of the month.
The HWY 6 Fire started in late July from unknown causes in Garfield County, and grew to 100 acres before it was contained the next day.
A funnel cloud was spotted by several people near Yampa.

The Colorado Department of Transportation reported flash flooding on Colorado Highway 340 at the west entrance to the Colorado National Monument. Up to 6 inches of water ran across the road as a result of heavy from thunderstorms. Additionally, some large boulder collapsed on the road as well as some mud. The superintendent of the Colorado National Monument also reported several inches of water flooded the Visitor's Center. Luckily, there were no injuries or damage to cars reported during the event. The rain gauge, located across from the Visitor's Center, recorded 0.90 inches of rain in 20 minutes.
A peak wind gust of 63 MPH was measured by an automated weather station 18 miles southeast of Massadona.
A peak wind gust of 62 MPH was measured by the automated weather station at the Cortez Municipal Airport.
A peak wind gust of 60 MPH was measured by the automated weather station at the Canyonlands Field Airport outside of Moab.
The Garfield County Sheriff's office reported flash flooding in portions of Carbondale as a result of heavy rain from thunderstorms.
A mudslide occurred up Sneve Gulch at Sylvan Lake as a result of heavy rain from thunderstorms.
Debris of mud and rock fell across portions of the Rio Grande Trail outside of Aspen as a result of heavy rain from thunderstorms.
Hail estimated to be an inch in diameter was reported on social media from Carbondale.

Strong thunderstorms sat over the Lake Christine Burn Scar with rain rates exceeding 1 inch per hour at times. As a result of heavy rain over the burn scar, there were reports of minor flooding in some townhomes. Additionally, the pedestrian underpass next to Whole Foods was filled with around 5.5 feet of water.
A peak wind gust of 60 MPH was measured by the automated weather station at the Canyonlands Field Airport outside of Moab.
The Dry Lake Fire started in early August from a lightning strike 3 miles east-northeast of Yellow Jacket Pass, and grew to 1372 acres before it was contained at the in mid August.
The Deserado Fire started in mid August from a lightning strike 8 miles east of Rangely, and grew to 1131 acres before it was contained the next week.
The Harvest Fire started in mid August from a lightning strike north of Rangely, and grew to 157 acres before it was contained the next week.
The Bunkwater Fire started in mid August from a lightning strike near De Beque Canyon just west of Interstate 70, and grew to 138 acres before it was contained the next week.
Standing water reported near the Paradox Valley Inn Bed and Breakfast. CoCoRaHS observer estimated at least 0.50 inches of rain fell in less than an hour.

A debris flow of mud and rocks occurred as a result of heavy rain over portions of the Grizzly Creek Fire burn scar. The debris flow took place near mile marker 120.6. The No Name Creek rain gauge reported 1.86 inches of rain fell in 50 minutes.
Flooding occurred in the parking lot near the Mesa Mall in Grand Junction. A local broadcast meteorologist reported the water reached to the top of a pickup truck's tires.
A local broadcast meteorologist reported several inches of water running down the intersection of North Avenue and 1st Street in Grand Junction as a result of heavy rain from thunderstorms.
Wind gusts estimated to be 70 mph downed power lines and knocked over some trees 1 mile west-southwest of Eckert.
Daniels Hill (a section of Gunnison County Road 3) was damaged and unpassable due to flooding from heavy rain. The road remained closed until the following afternoon.
The emergency manager reported that heavy rain from thunderstorms led to minor flooding across portions of Cortez, including some basements in homes along Highway 491 and Veterans Park.

Heavy rain from thunderstorms over the Grizzly Creek Fire burn scar resulted in the ponding of water along portions of I-70 with a mud and debris slide reported near mile marker 120.6 I-70 was closed in both directions from 1800 on the evening of the 24th to 0000 on the 25th.
Heavy rain from thunderstorms led to 6 inches of water flowing over 12th Street and Park Avenue in Rifle.
Heavy rain from thunderstorms flooded a basement at the intersection of 5th Street and Ute Avenue in Rifle.

Minor flooding occurred in portions of Steamboat Springs as a result of heavy rain from thunderstorms. A CoCoRaHS observer located 1 mile north-northwest of town measured 1.18 inches of rain in 30 minutes.

The Colorado Department of Transportation reported 4 separate mudslides occurred along portions of I-70 within the Grizzly Creek Fire burn scar as a result of heavy rain from thunderstorms. The slides took place east of Hanging Lake Tunnel and 30 cars were trapped in between the flows. The largest slide took place near the westbound exit ramp of Bear Ranch and was roughly 50 feet long and covered one lane. The radar estimated precipitation totals of 0.65 to 0.85 inches north of the interstate with 1.80 inches measured at the East Fork Dead Horse automated gauge. The road remained closed until early on the morning of the 27th.

The trail system above Glenwood Meadows in Glenwood Springs (located between the community center and Roaring Fork Transportation Authority facility) suffered damage due to debris flows from heavy rain.

An NWS employee reported 1 to 2 feet of standing water at the intersection of 7th Street and Riverside Parkway in Grand Junction as a result of heavy rain from thunderstorms. Various observers recorded close to or more than an inch of rain fell with storms.

A strong thunderstorm developed over the Grand Mesa before moving northward over I-70. This led to a significant rockslide occurring on the interstate near the Highway 65 junction, or near mile marker 49. The eastbound lanes were closed for a period of time with some of the rocks making it to the westbound lanes. Radar estimated 0.60 to 0.90 inches of rain fell.
Heavy rain from thunderstorms resulted in minor flooding/ponding of water on portions of I-70 near mile marker 56 going east towards De Beque.

Heavy rain from thunderstorms led to flooding across portions of County Road 95 (about 1/4 mile north of Moffat County Road 104) in western Moffat County. The road was impassable and closed shortly after.
Flooding was reported by Montrose County Dispatch near mile marker 87 on Highway 141 as a result of heavy rain from thunderstorms.

The emergency manager reported several inches of rain running through the streets of Cortez as a result of heavy rain from thunderstorms. The Cooperative Observer measured 0.55 inches of rain in 35 minutes.
The emergency manager reported flooding at the intersection of 25 and L Roads northeast of downtown Cortez as a result of heavy rain from thunderstorms.

A CoCoRaHS observer southwest of Redvale reported flooding as a result of heavy rain from thunderstorms. Over an inch of rain was recorded, which led to partial erosion of the observer's irrigation ditch.

Heavy rain from thunderstorms over the Mill Creek drainage resulted in a spillover on Powerhouse Dam in Grand County. Radar estimated 0.80 to 1.10 inches of rain fell over the North Fork Mill Creek drainage.
Some standing water accumulated on a portion of I-70 as a result of heavy rain from thunderstorms. Radar estimated over an inch of rain fell in 40 minutes.
A peak wind gust of 59 MPH was measured by the automated weather station at the Rifle Garfield County Airport.
Mud and debris flowed across County Road 17 at Corbett Creek near the Dallas Trailhead as a result of heavy rain from thunderstorms. The road remained closed through the end of the month.
Heavy rain from thunderstorms resulted in a debris flow in the Yankee Boy Basin area.
The Lead King Basin Loop Road, a 13-mile loop near Marble that travels through the Lead King Basin, experienced debris flows due to heavy rain from thunderstorms. The road was not accessible.

Accident involved a party of two backcountry skiers and a dog headed to an area known locally as Birthday Chute in the Pitkin Creek drainage, northeast of the town of Vail. They triggered the avalanche while climbing the slope, and were swept 2000 feet downhill. The first skier was partially buried but was able to self-extricate and suffered injury to their arm, the second skier was not buried but had injured both a leg and hand and was unable to move. The dog was partially buried but was freed by the first skier. The first skier was able to go for help, the second skier was airlifted to the hospital, and the dog was carried out by the rescue team.

The first two riders noticed that the third was no longer behind them.|The pair turned around and headed up the canyon and found a fresh avalanche that had buried the third snowmobiler. Numerous mesonet sites across Colorado Zone 003 reported wind gusts above high wind thresholds during the day on March 2nd. Reports of downed trees in the City of Grand Junction were received from the Grand Junction Fire Department, as well as numerous power outages across the valley according to Grand Valley Power. Two minor brush fires also occurred during this period of high winds, according the Grand Junction Fire Department, possibly sparked by arcing power lines and fanned by the strong winds.

The peak gust of 62 mph was recorded three times between two different sites. The earliest occurrence of this was recorded at the mesonet site 1 ESE Meeker at 10:38 AM, followed by both the mesonet site and the ASOS site KEEO recording gusts to 62 mph at 10:53 AM. events.cz_name: CENTRAL GUNNISON AND UNCOMPAHGRE RIVER BASIN
events.event_narrative: The Rattlesnake Gulch Fire started in mid April due to unknown causes 8 miles west of Delta in the Dominguez-Escalante National Conservation Area. The fire grew to 110 acres before it was contained in mid April. Seven power poles destroyed sending their lines into the Gunnison River, several hundred railroad ties damaged, and the historic Gunnison River waterwheel was heavily damaged with the wooden supports and flume destroyed. However, the wheel remains in tact.

Wind gusts across the zone ranged from 45 mph to 65 mph, with the peak gust of 65 mph occurring at the Hole N The Rock mesonet station just off of US Highway 191, about 15 miles south of Moab, UT. Three other sites also recorded wind gusts above 58 mph during this event.

Wind gusts across the zone ranged from 45 mph to 59 mph, with the peak gust of 59 mph occurring at the KCNY ASOS located at Canyonlands Airport. One other site also recorded a gust above 58 mph during this event.

Wind gusts across the zone  ranged from 45 mph to 65 mph, with the peak gust of 66 mph occurring at the Vernal CWOP station in Vernal, UT. Three additional sites recorded gusts above 58 mph during this event. The KVEL ASOS, located at the Vernal Airport, recorded a peak gust of 51 mph.

Wind gusts across the zone ranged from 45 mph to nearly 60 mph, with the peak gust of 58 mph recorded at the Monument Valley Utah Department of Transportation weather station. This was the only location to record a gust at or above 58 mph. The KBDG AWOS in Blanding, UT recorded a gust to 56 mph.

The peak wind gusts of 79 mph was recorded at the Colorado Department of Transportation weather station located near Basalt, CO. This was the only location in the zone to record a gust above 75 mph. The KASE ASOS recorded a peak gust of 45 mph.

This was the only location to record gusts above 58 mph. The KGJT ASOS at the Grand Junction Regional Airport recorded a peak gust of 55 mph.

events.cz_name: FOUR CORNERS / UPPER DOLORES RIVER BASIN
events.event_narrative: Reports of Blowing Dust across portions of Montezuma County, in Colorado Zone 021, with localized areas of visibility reduced to less that 1 mile. This blowing dust seemed to be concentrated around Sleeping Ute Mountain, and was focused at the surface level, with higher elevation vantage points providing improved visibility.

Winds across the zone ranged from 40 to 55 mph, with peak gust of 64 mph occurring in Palisade. This wind helped carry blowing dust that significantly reduced visibility across the zone, with much of the Grand Valley and the northern Gunnison valley being unable to see local landmarks such as Colorado National Monument, the Grand Mesa, and the Bookcliffs. Combinations of webcams, social media posts, and NWS employee reports indicate visibility was reduced to less that 1 mile.

Combinations of social media reports and web cam images from across the zone indicated dense areas of blowing dust, with visibility estimated to have been reduced to less than 1/2 mile. The worst of this was reported in and around the Monument Valley area of southeast Utah, where estimated winds of 45-55 mph lofted dust in from northern Arizona. Dust continued tracking north through the zone, but visibility improved above 1 mile based on various observation sources.

Localized pockets of dense fog developed across the Grand Valley during the early morning hours of April 28th. This included near the Grand Junction Regional Airport, where the KGJT ASOS reported visibilities less than 1/2 mile. In addition, localized pockets of dense fog formed along the Colorado River between Grand Junction and the town of Fruita to the west, impacting a portion of I-70 that runs along the river.

Minimum temperatures across the zone ranged from 32F to 16F, with the minimum temperature of 16F occurring at the Kane Gulch RAWS, KAGU1. 9 of the 10 available sites registered temperatures at or below 32 degrees for at least 3 hours, and these temperatures lasted for, on average, 8 hours during the event, which qualifies this as a Freeze Event. In addition, 5 of the available 10 sites registered temperatures at or below 28 degrees for at least 3 hours, with the average duration being 4.5 hours. This qualifies this event as a Hard Freeze event.

Minimum temperatures across the zone ranged from 32F to 23F. The minimum temperature of the event was 23F, recorded at the UTHAD site Harley Dome, at MP 226 on I-70. In addition, the KCNY ASOS at Canyonlands Airport recorded a minimum temperature of 25F. 8 of the available 16 sites recorded temperatures at or below 32F for at least 3 hours, with these temperatures lasting for on average 5.5 hours. Only 4 of the available 16 sites recorded temperatures at or below 28 degrees for at least 3 hours, with these sites seeing an average duration of 3.5 hours. Based on these data, this event in Utah Zone 027 qualifies only as a Freeze.

Minimum temperatures across the zone ranged from 32F to 23F during this event. The minimum temperature of 23F occurred at multiple sites, first at the mesonet site PC180, and then at the KBDG ASOS at Blanding Airport, in Blanding, UT. 6 of the 7 available sites recorded temperatures at or below 32F for at least 3 hours, with these temperatures lasting for, on average, 5 hours. Additionally, 5 of the 7 available sites recorded temperatures at or below 28F for at least 3 hours, with these lasting for on average 3.5 hours. These data indicate this zone experienced both a Freeze and a Hard Freeze event.

Minimum temperatures across the zone ranged from 32F to 23F during this event. The lowest recorded temperature of 23F occurred at two sites, AV979 and E8921, both mesonet sites. The KGJT ASOS at the Grand Junction regional airport recorded a minimum temperature of 27F. 15 of the 18 available sites recorded temperatures at or below 32F for at least 3 hours, with an average duration of 6 hours. Only 6 of the 18 sites recorded temperatures at or below 28 degrees for at least 3 hours, with an average duration of 3.5 hours. Based on these data, this event for this zone qualifies only as a Freeze.

With an unusually cold airmass in place, and calm winds and clear skies promoting effective radiational cooling, temperatures dropped below freezing across much of the zone. 7 of the 10 sites available recorded temperatures at or below 32F for at least 3 hours, with the average duration of these temperatures being 5 hours. Only 3 sites recorded temperatures at or below 28F for at least 3 hours, with an average duration being 2.5 hours. The lowest temperature recorded was 22F at a Colorado State Agricultural Mesonet station. The KRIL ASOS at the Garfield Regional Airport in Rifle, CO recorded a minimum temperature of 28F. Minimum temperatures ranged from 22F to 32F, with an average minimum of 29F. This event qualifies as a general Freeze, but not a Hard Freeze.

Reports from the City of Steamboat Springs on facebook informed followers that the Yampa River Core Trail would be closed periodically due to snowmelt flooding as river levels fluctuated. River levels during this period ranged from 3.5 ft to 4.5 ft, before dropping below 3 ft again.

The Spruce Creek Fire started in mid May from a lightning strike 15 miles northeast of Cortez. The fire grew to 5,699 acres before it was contained in late May. The fire is estimated to have cost $3 million.

The Leota Fire started in early to mid April from human causes 14 miles east-southeast of Randlett in the Ouray Wildlife Refuge Area. The fire grew to 137 acres before being contained the day after it started.

A peak wind gust of 68 MPH was measured by the automated weather station at the Eagle County Regional Airport. A tree was knocked down in Gypsum around the same time that these thunderstorm wind gusts occurred.
