events.cz_name: GORE AND ELK MOUNTAINS/CENTRAL MOUNTAIN VALLEYS
events.event_narrative: Generally 6 to 11 inches of snow fell across the southern half of the area at elevations above 11,000 feet. 6 to 8 inches of snow fell at the Snowmass and Aspen Ski Areas.
Generally 4 to 11 inches of snow fell across the northern half of the area at elevations above 11,000 feet. 10.5 inches of snow was measured at Crested Butte 6.2 N.

Winds across the region ranged from 45 mph to 60 mph during over the course of the multiday wind event, with the peak gust of 60 mph occurring on the afternoon of the 5th. This gust was recorded at the Dragon Road RAWS site.

Gusts ranged from 45 mph to 65 mph, with a peak gust of 66 mph occurring the KEEO ASOS in Meeker, CO on the afternoon of the 5th. Four of the 5 gusts over 58 mph occurred at the KEEO ASOS during this time frame. The other gust was 61 mph at the Pinto, Massadona 18SE RAWS, also on the afternoon of the 5th. The majority of peak gusts occurred on the 5th, although a few occurred with the cold frontal passage on the 7th.

Gusts ranged from 45 mph to 85 mph across the zone, with a peak recorded gust of 84 mph recorded at the Colorado Department of Transportation Mesonet site 139s034 Douglas Pass during the late morning on the 5th. This mesonet station recorded all four gusts over 75 mph, which all occurred on the 5th. Additional gusts under threshold but above 45 mph occurred with the cold front passage on the 7th, and a questionable wind gust to 141 mph at the Douglas Pass mesonet was recorded on the 6th.

Wind gusts across the zone ranged from 45 mph to 60 mph, with a peak gust of 61 mph recorded at the KGJT ASOS at the Grand Junction Regional Airport on the afternoon of the 5th. Peak gusts occurred mainly on the 5ht, although some gusts occurred with the cold frontal passage on the 7th. A total of 3 recorded gusts were at or above 58 mph.

events.cz_name: GORE AND ELK MOUNTAINS/CENTRAL MOUNTAIN VALLEYS
events.event_narrative: Wind gusts across the zone ranged from 45 mph to 85 mph, with the peak recorded gust of 85 mph occurring at the Colorado Department of Transportation Mesonet site 082w023 Basalt-Holland Hills. This higher elevation zone recorded wind gusts above 45 mph beginning late on the 4th and last through the afternoon of the 7th. Only one gust above 75 mph was recorded, but multiple gusts above 60 mph were recorded on each day.

events.cz_name: CENTRAL GUNNISON AND UNCOMPAHGRE RIVER BASIN
events.event_narrative: Wind gusts across the zone ranged from 45 mph to 60 mph, with the peak gusts of 60 mph both occurring at the Colorado Department of Transportation Mesonet site 050w054 Mesa County Line South on the afternoon of the 5th. The peak gust recorded at the KMTJ ASOS at the Montrose Regional Airport was 51 mph on the morning of the 7th. Additionally all the sites in this zone recorded gusts above 45 mph each day during this multiple day event.

Wind gusts across the zone ranged from 45 mph to 95 mph, with the peak gust of 96 mph being recorded at KMYP AWOS on Monarch Pass on the morning of the 7th. Peak gusts occurred just prior to cold frontal passage on the 7th, but gusts above 45 mph began occurring on the morning of the 5th. The other gust recorded above 75 mph was recorded on the morning of the 6th, also at KMYP, indicating that high winds occurred for the duration of this event here.

events.cz_name: FOUR CORNERS / UPPER DOLORES RIVER BASIN
events.event_narrative: Wind gusts across the zone ranged from 45 mph to 60 mph, with the peak gust of 60 mph recorded at the Colorado Department of Transportation Mesonet Station 491s068 Dove Creek on the afternoon of the 5th. This was the only gust above 58 mph, although numerous gusts into the 50s mph were recorded across the zone on all three days of the event. The peak gust recorded at KCEZ ASOS at the Cortez-Montezuma County Airport was 54 mph on the morning of the 5th.

Wind gusts across the zone ranged from 45 mph to near 60 mph during this event. The peak recorded gust of 58 mph occurred during the early morning hours of the 6th at KDRO ASOS at the Durango-La Plata County Airport. Peak gusts occurred during the late night hours of the 5th into the early morning hours of the 6th, with a secondary peak on the afternoon of the 7th associated with the cold frontal passage.

Gusts across the zone ranged from 45 mph to near 65 mph. The peak recorded gust was 62 mph on the evening of the 6th, recorded at a Citizen Weather Observation Program Mesonet site in Vernal. While this was the only recorded gust above 58 mph, gusts above 45 mph were recorded through the duration of the event, even into the post-cold frontal regime on the evening of the 7th. Peak gusts on the evening of the 6th were associated with the immediately pre-frontal airmass.

Wind gusts across the zone ranged from 45 mph to near 70 mph during this event. The peak gusts of 67 mph were both recorded on the evening of the 7th at KCNY ASOS at the Canyonlands Airport north of Moab. These peak gusts actually occurred in the post-frontal regime, but gusts of 50 mph were common from the evening of the 5th on through the cold frontal passage on the 7th.

Gusts across the zone ranged from 45 mph to 60 mph during this event. The peak gust of 60 mph was recorded at the Hole N The Rock Mesonet station located about 12 miles south of Moab on the afternoon of the 5th. 3 gusts of 58 mph or greater were recorded at this site on the 5th. The majority of peak gusts occurred on the 5th, with a secondary peak on the afternoon of the 7th associated with the cold front passage.

Wind gusts across the zone ranged from 45 mph to near 60 mph on the 17th and the 18th. The peak recorded wind gusts were both 58 mph, one recorded at the Great Divide 2SW RAWS on the evening of the 17th, and the other at the Pinto, Massadona 18SE RAWS on the evening of the 18th.

Wind gusts across the zone ranged from 45 mph to 85 mph. The peak gust of 85 mph occurred at the Pine Ridge, Cameo 6NW RAWS late on the evening of the 18th. The wind gusts across this zone seemed to peak as the shortwave was pushing the stalled front out of its position near the Wyoming border.
Winds across the zone ranged from 45 mph to near 65 mph. The peak recorded gust of 66 mph was recorded at KDRO ASOS at the Durango-La Plata County Airport on the evening of the 20th.

Wind gusts across the zone ranged from 45 mph to near 60 mph. The peak wind gust of 59 mph was recorded at the KCNY ASOS at the Canyonlands Airport, north of Moab. This was the only wind gust to be recorded above 58 mph.

As the cold front became more mobile on the 19th, portions of northeastern Utah experienced some high winds. Gusts across the zone ranged from 45 mph to near 60 mph. The peak gusts of 61 mph were recorded at the Utah Department of Transportation Mesonet site US-40 At Mp 140 Asphalt Ridge and at the Vernal West Mesonet station. Both of these gusts occurred in the early afternoon on the 19th.

Wind gusts across the zone ranged from 45 mph to near 65 mph during this event. The peak recorded wind gust was 64 mph at the Vernal Citizen Weather Observation Program mesonet location in Vernal, on the evening of the 23rd. Peak wind gusts occurred after the cold front passed and winds switched to northwesterly, with favors downsloping in that part of the Uinta Basin and enhances wind gusts.

Wind gusts across the zone ranged from 50 mph to near 70 mph. The peak gust was to 68 mph and occurred at KEGE AWOS at the Eagle County Regional Airport during the early afternoon on the 25th. This was the only gust above 58 mph. The recorded gusts were clustered in time, all occurring within about an hour and a half of each other, likely reflecting the period of passage of the cold front.

Wind gusts across the zone ranged from 45 mph to near 65 mph. The peak recorded gust was 66 mph at the KCNY ASOS at the Canyonlands Airport north of Moab. Peak gusts appear to have occurred in the post-frontal northwest flow.

Social media reports began in late April of nuisance flooding along the Yampa Core Trail, and by the end of the month of May the Grand Junction Service hydrologist visited the area and was able to confirm the flooding was ongoing. River levels increased above the roughly 3.5 foot threshold for this trail flooding on the 14th, and remained above this through the end of the month. Peak river height of roughly 5.25 feet occurred on the 21st before gradually decreasing. A secondary, smaller peak of 4.75 feet occurred on the 29th, likely enhanced by precipitation in the area.

Gusts across the eastern Uinta Mountains ranged from 45 mph to the peak gust of 75 mph during the day on the 17th. The peak gust was recorded at the Utah Department of Highways mesonet site Sr-43 at Mp 0.5 West Stateline, close to the Wyoming border, west of the town of Manila.

The peak gust associated with this thunderstorm was 58 mph and was recorded at the KCAG ASOS at the Craig-Moffat County Airport at 3:31 PM MDT. Additional gusts with this storm, while strong, were generally below severe criteria.
The Pinto RAWS station recorded a gust to 60 mph with a passing thunderstorm. This storm also produced a gust to 49 mph at the KEEO ASOS at Meeker Airport.

The Snow Ranch Fire started in early to mid June due to a lightning strike 11 miles west of Pagosa Springs in the San Juan Mountains. The fire grew to 386 acres before it was contained in late June. The estimated cost was $658,650 to date with a final cost of $1 million.

The Rabbit Valley Fire started in mid June due to human causes 9 miles west of Mack, Colorado, immediately north of Interstate 70 near the Colorado-Utah state line on the Colorado side. The fire grew to 1281.5 acres before being contained in mid to late June three days later. The estimated cost was $500,000.

Whenever enough moisture and instability is present, a thunderstorm forms along the Utah Tavaputs near the McCook Ridge RAWS site. On this day, this RAWS site captured a wind gust to 81 mph at 1:27 MDT from the nearby thunderstorm. This storm also likely produced some small hail, although the remoteness of the location makes verification of that exceptionally difficult.

With the increased monsoonal moisture at midlevels, scattered showers and thunderstorms built on the higher terrain near Cortez. Dry surface levels acted to enhance outflow winds as storms moved overhead. These storms eventually moved over Cortez, they produced gusts to 58 mph at the KCEZ ASOS at Cortez-Montezuma Airport in Cortez. Gusts to 58 mph were recorded twice, once at 1:02 PM MDT and again at 1:09 PM MDT.

Late in the day, a round of showers and thunderstorms moved east along the higher terrain of the central and upper Colorado River Valleys. These storms produced gusts above 45 mph, including one recorded gust to 58 mph at the Colorado Department of Transportation mesonet station 0.1 mile West of No Name Tunnel. An additional mesonet station approximately 12 miles to the east recorded a gust to 53 mph.
Report received of penny size hail 8 miles south-southwest of Meeker. Video of Highway 13 shows the road covered in hail after the storm moved through.

A thunderstorm moving over the city of Montrose late in the afternoon of the 24th produced strong to severe wind gusts, including one gust to 70 mph. This gust was recorded at the KMTJ ASOS at Montrose Regional Airport at 6:50 PM MDT. Damage was associated with this storm, with reports of several large tree limbs blown down.
Brief heavy rain was accompanied by pea size hail, which caused 1 inch of water to run over a portion of 8th street in Glenwood Springs. Amount of rain was unknown.

A thunderstorm developed near Green River, UT on the afternoon of the 25th and produced strong to severe wind gusts. Only one severe wind gust was recorded. This was 58 mph at the Utah Climate Center - AGMET mesonet site approximately 5 miles north of Green River. No reports of damages or fatalities were received.

A storm that formed near the Durango-La Plata County Airport produced heavy rainfall and strong, gusty winds as it moved through. Most recorded gusts were below severe thresholds, but one gust to 64 mph was recorded at the KDRO ASOS at 6:33 PM MDT. No reports of damages, injuries, or fatalities were received.

One of several strong to severe thunderstorms that passed through the city of Montrose produced a bolt of lightning that struck a house south of town. This then set the house on fire, eventually destroying it.

A severe thunderstorm that moved through mainly Grand Junction and suburbs of such, including the Redlands and Orchard Mesa, produced strong to severe wind gusts. The peak gust recorded at the KGJT ASOS at Grand Junction Regional Airport was 63 mph at 4:53PM MDT. Some reports of wind damage were recieved, including that of downed and broken trees, reported by a local television station.

A severe thunderstorm moved through portions of Moffat and Routt counties on the evening of the 21st, producing several forms of severe weather. The KCAG ASOS at Craig-Moffat County Airport recorded a severe wind gust to 66 mph at 6:19 PM MDT. This storm went on to cause damage near Hayden.

A severe thunderstorm that moved through Craig on the evening of the 21st produced several severe weather types, including winds. The peak gust was 66 mph, which was recorded at the KCAG ASOS at Craig-Moffat County Airport. In addition, at the nearby Loudy-Simpson Park, the Whittle the Wood festival sustained damage in the form of porta-potties and tents being blown over. In addition, multiple reports of downed limbs were received, some with a diameter of 4 inches.

A severe thunderstorm moved through the Hayden area on the evening of the 21st, bringing multiple severe threats including strong to severe winds. The peak gust recorded at KHDN AWOS at Hayden-Yampa Valley Airport was only 48 mph, but there were multiple reports of damage in Hayden proper. This included downed trees and limbs. Reports from local Law Enforcement indicated a tree down, blocking Maple Street. Another downed tree was reported to have crushed a parked car.

A severe thunderstorm forming on the nearby Abajo Mountains tracked over the city of Blanding in Southeast Utah, producing multiple severe weather hazards, including strong to severe winds. The peak recorded gust was 65 mph at KBDG AWOS at Blanding Municipal Airport, which occurred around 2 PM MDT. No reports of damage from wind were received.

A strong to severe thunderstorm moved through Vernal on the afternoon of the 21st, producing some strong wind gusts. The only severe wind gust recorded with this event was the 72 mph gust recorded at KVEL ASOS at the Vernal Airport at 4:12 PM MDT. No reports of wind damage were received with this event.

A severe thunderstorm moved through portions of Grand County on the evening of the 21st, producing severe winds in addition to other hazards. The strongest winds likely occurred south of the KCNY ASOS at Canyonlands Field, as the core of the storm moved through Moab, about 10 miles to the south. The peak recorded gust was 58 mph at KCNY ASOS at 5:37 PM MDT. No reports of damage due to winds alone were received.

A strong to severe thunderstorm moved through the far western portion of Mesa County in Colorado. A trained spotter measured a gust to 65 mph at her home, 5 miles northwest of Mack. In addition, an automated Colorado Department of Transportation mesonet site recorded a gust to 57 mph near the Utah state line on I-70. This is roughly 10 miles southwest of the spotter's location. No reports of wind damage were received.

A severe thunderstorm moved over the city of Montrose, producing multiple severe threats including winds. The peak recorded gusts were both 62 mph, and both were recorded at the KMTJ ASOS at Montrose Regional Airport. These gusts were measured at 5:20 PM MDT and 5:40 PM MDT. Gusts with this storm ranged from 45 mph to the peak of 62 mph. No reports of damage were received.

An area of strong to severe thunderstorms moved over the Blanding area in Southeast Utah on the afternoon of the 27th. In addition to other severe threats, this storm produced some severe winds, including 2 recorded gusts to 69 mph at the KBDG AWOS at the Blanding Municipal Airport. These gusts were recorded at 4:31 PM MDT and 4:35 PM MDT. No reports of damage from wind were received.

A strong to severe thunderstorm tracked from west to east along I-70 on the afternoon of the 27th, producing strong to severe wind gusts in addition to other hazards. Wind gusts ranged from 45 mph to 61 mph. The peak gust of 61 mph was recorded at the Utah Department of Transportation mesonet site I-70 at MP 226 Harley Dome. This was the only location to see a severe wind gust with this storm, although this same storm did go on to produce more severe wind gusts at locations just to the east, in Mesa County, CO. No reports of wind damage were received with this storm.
Rainfall amount of 0.37 inches fell in 10 to 15 minutes causing minor street flooding in Fruita as drains could not keep up. Rates were 1 to 2 inch per hour.
Heavy rain caused water to run off a dirt slope above town, causing minor street flooding in town. Video posted on X.

Multiple photos and videos on social media from multiple angles indicated a brief spin up of a landspout on Highway 191 near Hole N The Rock, or about 16 miles south of Moab, UT. No damage was reported.
A severe thunderstorm moved through the Durango east area producing hail from half inch to a little over quarter size.

A severe thunderstorm moved across the Grand Junction area from downtown to the airport, producing 0.75 to 1 inch diameter hail. Hail caused some damage with skylights broken at the Walmart on the south side of town.

A strong to severe thunderstorm tracked down the Colorado National Monument, across the Redlands, portions of downtown Grand Junction and over the Grand Junction Regional Airport. The GJT ASOS at the Grand Junction Regional Airport recorded 1.07 inches of rain with rainfall rates of 1 inch in 30 minutes and there were several reports of hail/accumulation of hail. Heavy rain resulted in 6 to 8 inches of water running over some downtown Grand Junction streets, in parking lots and topping the curbs. There was standing water along River Road with lots of small hail contributing to drainage issues. Leach Creek near Catalina Drive filled with debris once water reached the HOA, resulting in flooding.
Public reported measured hail of 1.5 inches in downtown Moab at 3:18 PM MDT in association with a severe thunderstorm. No reports of damage received.
Local emergency management in Moab reported hail just shy of an inch in association with a severe thunderstorm moving over the area. No reports of hail damage were received.
Public reported 1 inch hail in downtown Moab in association with a severe thunderstorm moving through the area.
A trained spotter reported 1.0 inch hail in association with a severe thunderstorm that moved through Moab on the afternoon of the 27th.
Public reported an estimated hail size of 1.0 inches, comparable to a quarter, in association with a severe thunderstorm moving over Moab. No hail damage was reported.
Trained spotter reported 1.0 inch hail in association with a severe thunderstorm that moved over the Moab area on the afternoon of the 27th. No damage was reported.

COOP Observer reported hail of an estimated 0.88 inches, comparable to a Nickle, in the Orchard Mesa area southeast of Grand Junction on the afternoon of the 27th. This hail was reported to have caused damaged to crops within a roughly 2 mile radius.
Public reported an estimated hail size of 1.0 inches in association with a severe thunderstorm moving over the Moab area on the afternoon of the 21st. No damage was reported.
Trained Spotter reported 1.0 inch hail in addition to heavy rain associated with a severe thunderstorm moving through the Moab area on the afternoon of the 21st.
A COOP Observer near La Sal, UT reported 1 inch hail in association with a severe thunderstorm that passed over the area on the morning of the 21st.

Major flooding in Moab and Castle Valley from strong thunderstorm that produced very heavy rain across town, Mill Creek, North Mill Creek, Kane Creek and a drainage above Castle Valley. 1 inch of rain fell in 15 minutes for a rainrate of 4 inches per hour. 2 reported missing in Moab area with an abandoned vehicle discovered in Mill Creek drainage after flash flooding, 1 was found deceased and other assumed fatality but not found.

Significant flooding occurred due to heavy rains from a thunderstorm near Valley of the Gods and northeast of Mexican Hat. Fast moving waters covered Highway 163 near Valley of the Gods for a distance of 540 meters and 1 meter deep. Cottonwood Wash had major flood, surrounding house and filling flood plain. San Juan River spiked from 8.3 ft (2670 cfs) to 17.99 ft (20,700 cfs) near Mexican Hat. 28 people were trapped and stranded while on a river trip on the San Juan River where Lime Creek enters and eventually rescued. However, their boats and gear were swept away and lost in floodwaters.
A strong storm produced heavy rain and caused a rockslide on Highway 50 eastbound between County Road 888 and County Road 237B at mile point 192.

Heavy rain from thunderstorms occurred in the early morning hours of June 21 and caused a major rock slide that damaged part of the railroad track for the Durango to Silverton Narrow Gauge Railroad. Exact time of occurrence is estimated. Part of the 45-mile long railroad track was blocked by a pile of debris after a rock slide occurred. Officials were notified about the rock slide just after 7:30 a.m. MDT that morning. The rock slide happened near mile post 486 just outside Needleton, which is about 55 minutes south of Silverton by train.
Heavy rain caused a mudslide across Highway 64 at mile marker 65 over Rio Blanco County, 11 miles west-southwest of Meeker.

A severe thunderstorm moved over the Moab area on the afternoon of the 27th, putting down very heavy rain and high rain rates. This caused flooding and debris flows across the area, including near Arches National Park. Flooding and debris flows outside the park on Highway 191 led to the closure of the road. Additionally, there were reports and photos of flooding and rockfalls/debris flows within the park on the scenic drive. These flows made the only entrance/exit road from the park impassable for a period of time.

A strong thunderstorm moved through Gateway with heavy rain rates of 1 to 3 inches per hour, where 1.18 inches of rain fell in a 30 minute period.  Flooding occurred due to the heavy rain rates where water moved wood and rocks into a nearby creek.  Internet service was lost during this time.

Heavy rainfall from strong to severe thunderstorms moved over the Moab area, causing flash flooding through the downtown Moab streets as well as the Mill Creek drainage where water was running over a few of the roads. Rainfall estimates of 0.8 to 1.5 inches fell during this time. Hail also accompanied the heavy rain with some hail up to quarter size.

A thunderstorm produced heavy rain over the Crystal River Drainage, which caused a mudslide on Highway 133 between mile markers 45 and 46 to the west of Marble, Colorado. Between 0.3 and 0.8 inches of rain was estimated on radar.

The Speirs Fire started in mid July due to a lightning strike 3 miles south of Dutch John, Utah which is south of the Flaming Gorge Reservoir. The fire grew to 715 acres before it was contained in mid to late August. The estimated cost was $9,609,000 to date.

The Speirs Fire started in mid July due to a lightning strike 3 miles south of Dutch John, Utah which is south of the Flaming Gorge Reservoir. The fire grew to 715 acres before it was contained in mid to late August. The estimated cost was $9,609,000 to date.

The Jones Fire started in mid July due to a lightning strike 7 miles south of I-70 near the Colorado/Utah state line in the Black Ridge Wilderness of the McInnis National Conservation Area. The fire grew to 215 acres before it was contained in mid to late July. The estimated final cost was $650,000.

The Currant Creek Fire started in late July due to unknown causes 5 miles northwest of Cedaredge, Colorado. The fire grew to 193 acres before it was contained in early August. The estimated final cost was $5 million.

The Currant Creek Fire started in late July due to unknown causes 5 miles northwest of Cedaredge, Colorado. The fire grew to 193 acres before it was contained in early August. The estimated final cost was $5 million.

The Kings Canyon Fire started in late July due to a lightning strike a half mile south of the Little Dolores River near Kings Canyon about 15 miles southwest of Fruita, Colorado. The fire grew to 220 acres before it was contained in early August. The estimated final cost was $1 million.

The Kings Canyon Fire started in late July due to a lightning strike a half mile south of the Little Dolores River near Kings Canyon about 15 miles southwest of Fruita, Colorado. The fire grew to 220 acres before it was contained in early August. The estimated final cost was $1 million.
Heavy rain rates from a thunderstorm resulted in mudslides across Highway 133 about 4 miles north of Redstone, resulting in a closure of the highway.

Heavy rainfall rates from a strong thunderstorm caused a mudslide to occur near Sawpit along Highway 145 between mile markers 76 and 80. This mudslide resulted in a closure of Highway 145 in both directions.

Heavy rainfall rates of 0.5 to 1 inch in less than an hour from a strong thunderstorm resulted in flash flooding in Hells Canyon through Dinosaur National Monument. An additional inch accumulation of pea sized hail also accompanied the heavy rain resulting in the flash flooding.

Heavy rain from slow moving thunderstorms resulted in multiple mudslides along Highway 145 between mile markers 72 and 77, south of Sawpit. There were reports of 4 mudslides between mile markers 72 and 77 on Highway 145 between 1545 and 1600 MST. One, possibly two, bigger slides occurred between mile markers 76 and 77 on Highway 145. This resulted in a closure of Highway 145 between mile markers 72 and 78 in both directions.
Heavy rainfall rates from a strong thunderstorm resulted in mudslides along Highway 550 to the north of Durango, reducing traffic to one lane.

Heavy rain from strong thunderstorms resulted in a rock slide across Highway 151 in an area between the intersection of Forest Service Road 618 and Highway 160. Colorado Highway 151 was closed in both directions due to the rock slide between mile markers 32 and 33.

A strong thunderstorm produced heavy rainfall rates resulting in a large mudslide at Avalanche Ranch along Highway 133.  There were other mudslides along Highway 133 between Redstone Blvd and Red Dog Rd about 4 miles north of Redstone. These mudslides resulted in Highway 133 being closed in both directions from mile markers 53 to 57.

The Babylon Fire started in early July due to a lightning strike 20 miles northwest of Blanding, Utah in the Manti-La Sal National Forest of the Abajo Mountains. The fire grew to 199 acres before it was contained in mid July. The estimated final cost was $500,000.

One of several thunderstorms across Southeast Utah on the afternoon of July 20th began to rotate and produced a landspout tornado near Verdure in San Juan County, UT, along US Highway 191. This landspout was reported to the Grand Junction NWS office by a trained spotter, and this report was later confirmed by images and video provided by a media partner in the Salt Lake City NWS office's area.

On the afternoon of the 11th, one of the storms drifting south off the San Juan mountains produced a wind gust to 60 mph over the Durango-La Plata County Airport. This gust was recorded by the KDRO ASOS at the airport. No other gusts of this magnitude were recorded, and no reports of damage or injury were received.

Showers and thunderstorms initially formed over the adjacent higher terrain of the eastern Uinta Mountains, before drifting over the Uinta Basin. As these storms moved over the town of Vernal, they produced wind gusts of 45-60 mph. The peak wind gust of 60 mph was recorded at the KVEL ASOS at Vernal Airport. No reports of damage or injury were received.

Showers and thunderstorms formed off the higher terrain in the western half of Moffat County, and gradually drifted east. As it did so, these storms produced a wind gust to 71 mph, that was recorded by the Mesonet site GDRC2, 2 miles southwest of Great Divide. This was the only recorded gust of this strength. No reports of injuries or damage were received.

A round of showers and thunderstorms tracked across central Rio Blanco county, producing wind gusts ranging from 45 to 60 mph. The peak recorded gust was 58 mph, and this was recorded at KEEO ASOS, located at Meeker Airport. No reports of damages or injuries were received.

Thunderstorms tracked across Rio Blanco and Routt counties on the afternoon of the 27th, producing strong to severe wind gusts as they did so. Recorded wind gusts ranged from 50 mph to 60  mph, with the peak gust being recorded at the PIRC2 Pinto mesonet site, 18 miles southeast of Massadona. Gusts into the 50s were recorded at KEEO ASOS at Meeker Airport and KHDN AWOS at Yampa Valley Airport in Hayden. No reports of damages or injuries were received.

Showers and thunderstorms formed over the higher terrain of northeastern Utah on the afternoon of August 7. As these storms developed, there were enhanced by some upper level support in the form of a passing wave and an upper level jet. This allowed the storms to grow strong enough to potentially produce severe threats, such as wind in excess of 58 mph and hail in excess of 1 inch. Additionally, dry surface layers would enhance already potentially strong outflow winds. All this combined to produce a 90 mph gust at the Winter Ridge RAWS, located in the Utah Tavaputs Plateau. No reports of damage or injuries were received.

With just enough moisture to work with, showers and thunderstorms began to form on the higher terrain around the Uinta Basin early in the afternoon of August 7. These storms received some upper level support in the form of a passing shortwave and a modest upper level jet, which allowed them to become strong to severe. In addition, dry surface levels acted to boost already strong to severe winds. Winds recorded during this event ranged from 45 mph to the peak of 64 mph, which was recorded at a Utah State Climate Mesonet Site 9.1 miles east of Randlett. No reports of damage or injuries were received.

As the afternoon moved into evening, convection that had fired over the terrain in northeastern Utah gradually moved into northwest Colorado. Enhanced by a passing shortwave and a modest upper level jet, these showers and storms were capable of producing strong to severe winds, which were only enhanced by dry surface levels. Gusts associated with this event ranged from 45 mph to the peak of 60 mph, which was recorded at the KRIL ASOS at Garfield Regional Airport in Rifle. No reports of damage or injuries were received.

The Bucktail Fire started in early August 4 miles northeast of Nucla. The cause remains undetermined. The fire grew to 7,202 acres before it was contained in late August. The estimated final cost was $10 million.

Despite the saturated atmospheric profile, the strong to severe storms that developed on the afternoon of August 10 that were capable of producing severe winds. The peak gust with this storm was 59 mph, recorded twice at KDRO ASOS at the Durango-La Plata County Airport. This storm also produced heavy rain. No reports of damages or injuries were received.

The Big Gulch Fire started in early August 12 miles west of Craig due to a lightning strike. The fire grew to 1,161 acres before it was contained a couple days later in early August. The estimated cost to date was $150,000.

A thunderstorm that developed on the higher terrain of the western edge of the Uncompahgre Plateau moved over the Colorado Department of Transportation's Mesonet site 070w001 Utah State Line. This mesonet site recorded a wind gust to 61 mph with this storm, likely due to dry surface layers enhancing outflow winds. No reports of damages or injuries were received.

The Black Ridge Fire started in late August 40 miles north-northeast of Castle Valley in the Westwater Canyon Wilderness Area near the Utah-Colorado state line just south of Interstate 70 due to a lightning strike. The fire grew to 305 acres before it was contained a couple days later in late August. The estimated cost to date was $75,000.

A thunderstorm that formed over the higher terrain south and west of Canyonlands Airport in eastern Utah eventually drifted over the adjacent lower terrain. As it did so, it produced two wind gusts to 58 mph, in addition to wind gusts of lower values. These gusts were recorded at KCNY ASOS at Canyonlands Airport, 16 miles northwest of Moab. No reports of damages or injuries were received.

Despite the well saturated atmosphere, other parameters contributed to the development of a strong to severe thunderstorm over southern La Plata county. In addition to heavy rainfall, this storm produced a wind gust to 63 mph at the KDRO ASOS at Durango-La Plata County Airport. No reports of damage or injury were received in association with this gust.

Heavy rain due to thunderstorms over the area resulted in 1.5 to 2 inch per hour rainfall rates with pea size hail mixed in. This resulted in flooding across downtown Moab with 2 feet of water flowing through downtown. Mill Creek saw a rise in water levels which runs through town with water cresting the roadway bridge. Water was also seen running over some driveways.
A strong to severe storm passed over Thompson Springs and produced hail ranging from 0.7 to 1.25 inches in diameter.
A strong thunderstorm passed over the Fry Canyon area and produced hail up to nickel size.

Multiple mudslides were reported by local law enforcement near Redstone, CO. These mudslides followed the Crystal River valley, along State Highway 133 near mile marker 53. This is roughly 1 mile north of Redstone. Slow storm motion, steep terrain, and heavy rain all combined in an area known to be susceptible to debris flows and mudslides. Highway 133 was closed for several hours for cleanup.
Colorado Department of Transportation reported a mudslide on Interstate 70 at mile marker 159, between the towns of Wolcott and Edwards, necessitating a brief closure to clear the road.
Part of the same storm that led to a mudslide on Interstate 70. This mudslide impacted the Brush Creek Road area south of Eagle, CO. Road and bridge crews were dispatched to clear this area.

Part of the same storms that led to a mudslide on Interstate 70. Mudslides were reported along Squaw Creek Drive in Cordillera, south of Edwards. Road and bridge crews were dispatched to clean up the debris.
A strong thunderstorm passed over Naples area in Uintah County and produced hail up to nickel size.

Heavy rain from a slow moving storm over the Vail Pass area of Interstate 70 resulted in a small mud or rock slide early in the afternoon of August 5th. This slide was spotted via Colorado Department of Transportation webcams, and did result in a brief closure of one lane of Interstate 70 for cleanup.
A strong storm passed over Castle Valley area and produced hail dime to penny size.

Heavy rains from a thunderstorm fell upstream of Indian Creek and Salt Creek Wash between 1630 and 1800. Water flowed through both Indian Creek and Salt Creek Wash where it intersects with Highway 211 in Canyonlands National Park Needles District causing flash flooding with water flowing rapidly through the washes with some small tree branches.
Heavy rain from a thunderstorm caused a mudslide on Highway 64 at mile marker 57, approximately 17 miles west of Meeker.
Heavy rain from a thunderstorm produced a minor mudslide on Highway 82 at mile marker 12, about 1 mile north of Carbondale.

Heavy rain from a thunderstorm produced a mudslide along Highway 50 between mile marker 181 and 182 which closed the highway in both directions. This occurred approximately 25 miles east of Gunnison or 7 miles south-southwest of Waunita Hot Springs.
Heavy rain from a thunderstorm resulted in mud and small rocks across Highway 139 near Douglas Pass.

Highway 82 closed due to a mudslide as a result of heavy rain near Cattle Creek. Road was closed around 1941 on August 10th and remained closed until the morning of August 11th. This occurred approximately 2 miles northwest of Cattle Creek.

The Colorado Department of Transportation reported a closure along US Highway 50 roughly 10 miles east-southeast of Waunita Hot Springs, in Gunnison County. This area is on the climb up to Monarch Pass, meaning it is an area of very steep terrain that can be prone to rock and mudslides with heavy rainfall. The road had to be briefly closed for cleanup of the debris.

Heavy rains resulted in erosion of the Highway 141 bridge at mile marker 85.6 over Mesa Creek, roughly 8 miles northwest of Uravan. CDOT closed Highway 141 in both directions on August 12 at 1010 MST, nearly 24 to 36 hours after the inciting debris flow and scouring due to the compromised bridge.

Steady heavy rains during the evening of August 11th resulted in multiple mudslides and flooding overnight in east Telluride, Bridal Veil Falls Area and Tomboy Road. This resulted in closures of several nearby passes including from the East Spur at the Town of Telluride entrance east to Black Bear, Black Bear Pass itself, Tomboy Road and Imogene Pass. Time of event was based on radar estimate.

Early in the afternoon of August 18th, Law Enforcement reported a mudslide on Colorado State Highway 145 at mile marker 83, or about 3 miles north of the town of Sawpit or 1.5 miles south of the town of Placerville. This is an area well known for mudslides and debris flows with heavy rainfall thanks to very steep terrain. Time of incident was based on radar data, as Law Enforcement report came in after the fact. Road was closed for a short while to facilitate cleanup.

Colorado Department of Transportation reported the closure of Colorado State Highway 149 at mile marker 74, roughly 1 mile north-northwest of Lake City, due to a mudslide. This area is very steep, and prone to rock and mudslides with either prolonged moderate to heavy rainfall, or short but intense heavy rainfall.

Heavy rain from thunderstorms in Ouray caused town flooding as well as the flooding of several creeks including Oak, Cascade and Skyrocket Creek. These creeks filled with debris, rock and silt, resulting in trail closures and large boulders/rock slides and mudslides on Highway 550 at mile marker 94, 94.5 and 94.6 specifically but generally between mile markers 94 and 95 approximately 2 miles north-northwest of Ouray.  Storm total rainfall ranged from 1.5 to 1.7 inches in Ouray. Daily spot forecasts were requested by emergency management for both Ridgway and Ouray for extensive cleanup efforts for several days following the debris flows.

Colorado Department of Transportation reported Colorado State Highway 64 closed at mile marker 56, between Wray Gulch Road and Indian Valley, due to a mudslide. This was just north of White River City, or 18 miles west of the town of Meeker along Highway 64. The road remained closed for several hours while cleanup was undertaken. This stretch of Highway 64 runs along the base of a steep cliff, leaving it prone to debris and mudflows during intense, heavy rainfall events.

Heavy rainfall resulted in mudslides along Highway 550 at mile marker 101.5, approximately 2 miles south-southeast of Ridgway. About an inch of storm total rainfall was reported in Ridgway with this event. Daily spot forecasts were requested by emergency management for both Ridgway and Ouray for extensive cleanup efforts for several days following the debris flows.

Colorado Department of Transportation reported a mudslide and subsequent road closure of Colorado State Highway 82 at approximately mile marker 11, or between Satank Road turn off and Colorado State Highway 133. The road was closed for roughly 2 hours, reopening by 00:15AM MDT, or 23:15 MST. Colorado State Highway 82 in the vicinity of Carbondale is known to be susceptible to flash flooding and mud and debris flows will heavy, intense rainfall.

Public reported water, rocks, mud, and other debris over Colorado State Highway 139 between mile markers 29 and 30, or about 5 miles south-southeast of Douglas Pass. The area around and south of Douglas Pass is very steep and prone to rock, mud, and debris flows under heavy, intense rainfall such as what fell on the afternoon of August 25th.

Heavy rainfall to the northeast of Mesa Verde National Park fell on the afternoon of August 25th, with estimated rainfall rates in excess of 2 inches per hour for around 10 minutes. That puts the rainfall total along County Road 41, in this area, at 0.25-0.35 inches. The debris flow resulted in the closure of the road and damage to the road in at least 2 locations.

The Prairie Fire started in mid September 19 miles west-northwest of Mack, Colorado just north of Interstate 70 on the Utah side near the Colorado-Utah stateline due to a lightning strike. The fire grew to 1,921 acres before it was contained a couple days later in mid September. The estimated cost to date was $375,000.

Emergency manager for Montezuma County reported a large boulder loosened from multiple consecutive days of heavy rain having fallen onto Road G, near the intersection of Road 21, about 2.5 miles from Cortez-Montezuma County Airport. This large boulder necessitated heavy machinery to clean up, but did not impact traffic on the road, despite partially blocking the west-bound lane.

Occurred at the Browns Park National Wildlife Refuge Headquarters location. Small hail mixed with heavy rain fell initially until larger stones fell up to golf ball size. Vehicles have damage, garden destroyed and chicken coop is full of holes. Accumulation of hail plugged up some of the culverts.

Heavy Rainfall just east, northeast of Towaoc resulted in debris flows across Highline ditch/canal. Debris flow with mud and large boulders were noted near mile marker 29 on Highway 491 (between 21 Rd and B Rd).
A thunderstorm wind gust of 59 mph was measured at a Mesonet station 1 mile west-southwest of Douglas Pass at 1256 MST.
A thunderstorm wind gust of 63 mph was measured at the Durango La Plata County Airport at 825 MST.
A thunderstorm wind gust of 59 mph was measured at the Meeker Coulter Field Airport at 823 MST.
Thunderstorm wind gust of 58 mph was measured at the Sunlight Mountain AWOS observation site at 1255 MST.

A severe thunderstorm moved through 8 miles west of Ignacio and tracked to the northeast at 30 mph.  Path and time was estimated based on the Severe Thunderstorm Warning issued. Thunderstorm wind damage occurred with downed trees, a bent electric pole and a twisted power pole.  Property damage occurred in which an RV camper was smashed in half from the downed trees. Uncertain if this was tornado or straight line wind/downburst damage but leaning downburst winds.
A thunderstorm wind gust of 63 mph was measured at the Canyonlands Regional Airport.
Visibilities decreased to one quarter mile or less along the Colorado River and Interstate 70 from Mack to Grand Junction.
Strong winds from the south shifted to the north northeast and increased in intensity which caused tree limb damage.

events.cz_name: GORE AND ELK MOUNTAINS/CENTRAL MOUNTAIN VALLEYS
events.event_narrative: A nearly stationary thunderstorm over the Roaring Fork Valley produced heavy rain causing the ground to become saturated, which resulted in mudslides.  Several mudslides were reported along highway 82 between mile markers 27 and 30.  Mudslides also occurred along Woody Creek Road just below the town of Lenado.  A vehicle became trapped in one of the mudslides.  A rockslide also occurred near Independence Pass.
Heavy rain resulted in minor flooding of two homes along Lower River Road near mile marker 27.
Rainfall of 0.67 inches occurred.

The Tschuddi Fire started in early to mid September 16 miles west-northwest of Meeker, Colorado due to a lightning strike. The fire grew to 550 acres before it was contained in late October. The estimated final cost was $185,000.

The Tschuddi Fire started in early to mid September 16 miles west-northwest of Meeker, Colorado due to a lightning strike. The fire grew to 550 acres before it was contained in late October. The estimated final cost was $185,000.

The Verdure Creek Fire started in mid October 6 miles southwest of Monticello, Utah about a half mile north of the Blue Mountain Estates ranch home subdivision due to an undetermined cause. The fire grew to 157 acres before it was contained in late October. The estimated final cost was $3 million. The homes were not impacted as fire crews were able to contain and suppress the fire.
The Asbury Creek Fire started in mid October 7 miles north-northeast of Palisade, Colorado due to a lightning strike. The fire grew to 145 acres before it was contained in a day later in mid October.
Heavy rainfall up to 0.50 inches fell in 10 minutes. Pea-sized hail also occurred.
Thunderstorm wind gust caused a lot of blowing dust and prevented aircraft from departing the Durango-La Plata County Airport.
Lightning struck a power grid and knocked out power.
Nickel-sized hail occurred in East Glenwood Canyon.
Heavy rainfall caused two mud slides along highway 145 between Telluride and Placerville.
Heavy rain caused a mudslide near a residential area of Placerville.
Heavy rain caused debris flows and minor flooding along highway 240 south of Lemon Dam.  Roads were temporarily closed.

Flash flooding caused debris and water to flow over Highway 43 between mile markers 2 and 3.  Several inches of water was also reported running across Highway 44. Big rocks also fell across roadways near Sheep Creek.  A lot of debris flowed into nearby canals, and the Sheep Creek irrigation canal overflowed.  A dirt road to Sols Canyon was washed out, as well as E. 3rd Road in Manila, and a settling pond was also washed out.  Flooding also damaged several fields of crops, fences, landscaping, and irrigation systems.  Water and mud entered a church basement and garages of some residences.  Hail also caused crop damage.  Rainfall of 2 inches in 1 hour was reported.
Heavy rainfall of 1.5 inches fell within a 100 minute time period.

The ASOS at Craig-Moffat County Airport (KCAG) reported dense fog conditions with visibility under 1/4 for two hours during this period, while the KHDN AWOS at Yampa Valley Airport was in and out of dense fog during this period. The Colorado Avalanche Information Center provided all the information regarding this fatal avalanche accident. The incident occurred in the Northwest San Juan Mountains, on the slopes of Red Mountain #3. The snowpack in this location was known to be weak, and the avalanche danger on the day of the accident was rated as Moderate, or 2/5 on a scale where 1 is the least danger and 5 is the most danger. The victim of the accident, referred to as Skier 1 from here on, was travelling alone although they had arranged a check in system with their spouse. After completing several clean runs, Skier 1 triggered an avalanche that caught and buried them under approximately 1 meter of snow, which prevented self-excavation under the circumstances. When Skier 1 became overdue for the scheduled check-in with their spouse, the spouse notified search and rescue teams, and went to search for their spouse on their own. The spouse found Skier 1 buried and, with the help of nearby backcountry skiers and Ouray Mountain Rescue Team, were able to remove Skier 1 from the avalanche debris. However, Skier 1 had been buried for 4 or more hours, and had unfortunately passed away.

The Colorado Avalanche Information Center (CAIC) rated the avalanche danger at this location on the day of the incident as Moderate (2/5), with persistent slab avalanches being the main concern. The likelihood of an avalanche was rated as Possible and the expected size was Small to Large (up to D2), large enough to injure, bury, or kill. The period from late November to early February was generally dry, leading to a weak,  low cohesion snowpack onto which 3-4 feet of fresh snow fell from February 14th to the 19th. The incident party was made up of 2 experienced backcountry tourers. Rider 2 was very familiar with the terrain in the area, while this was Skier 1's first time in this area. They had toured together multiple times in other locations prior to this trip. Both read the avalanche forecast on the morning of the incident, and had made a plan to ski lower angle terrain to start, to test the snowpack for any signs of instability. Both had transceivers and carried avalanche probes and shovels. The incident party made for the steeper terrain of a feature known as The Nose in the afternoon. Skier 1 started his descent and within 5-10 second triggered an avalanche that caught him, but he was able to escape the avalanche 150-200 vertical feet below his starting point. Once out of the avalanche he looked and called for Rider 2 and received no response. Skier 1 began a transceiver search and, after about an hour of searching the widely spread out avalanche debris, finally located Rider 2, buried under about 6 feet of snow. An additional pair of rescuers had noticed the fresh avalanche and arrived in the area, searching on their own before finding Skier 1 and helping dig out Rider 2. When found, Rider 2 was not breathing and had no pulse. Rider 2 was finally fully excavated about 90 minutes after the avalanche, and while Silverton Medical Rescue arrived and provided care, even airlifting them to the hospital in Silverton, Rider 2 was pronounced dead.

The Colorado Avalanche Information Center rated the avalanche danger at this location on the day of the incident as Moderate (2/5), with persistent slab avalanches being the main concern. The likelihood of an avalanche was rated as Possible and the expected size was Large to Very Large (up to D3), large enough to not only bury, injure, or kill a person but also to bury cars, destroy a house, or break trees. The period from late November through early February had been generally dry, punctuated by strong but brief winter storms. In the week prior to this event, a major winter storm had brough a fresh 3-4 feet of snow to the area, along with light accumulations on subsequent days. This led to a weak, unstable snowpack that had already resulted in two fatal avalanche accidents in the days prior. On the day of the accident, two backcountry skiers had opted to ski an area know locally as Mine Dump, a steep, north-facing slope west of the town of Ophir, CO. Skier 1 triggered an avalanche in the upper snowpack that then stepped down to deep weak layers twice before reaching the ground. This avalanche caught skier one and carried him into a tree, injuring him. Skier 2, who was not caught, alerted a friend via radio, and the friend alerted San Miguel County Search and Rescue. San Miguel County Search and Rescue freed Skier 1 and evacuated him to a waiting ambulance, which later transferred him to a helicopter to airlift him to hospital.

A significant winter storm brought snow to much of eastern Utah and western Colorado. These patches of dense fog were isolated and transient, with sensors going in and out of dense fog conditions.

This injurious avalanche occurred south of the town of Marble, CO, off of a terrain feature know as Raspberry Ridge, in a run known locally as Money Shot. The Colorado Avalanche Information Center (CAIC) rated the avalanche danger in this area as Considerable (3/5) near and above treeline. CAIC's synopsis said dangerous avalanche conditions exist and indicated that slopes with a northerly component were the most dangerous, with the possibility of triggering a deadly avalanche on any of these slopes. Below treeline, the avalanche danger was listed as Moderate (2/5). The avalanche types of concern were Persistent Slab and Wind Slab. The accident slope on the 8th was steep, high elevation, and faced northeast, all factors that, per CAIC's forecast, made this a dangerous to deadly slope. In addition, this slope was known to be significantly more shallow than nearby slopes, and had a history of avalanching multiple times earlier in the 2024/2025 winter season. In fact, just the day before two backcountry tourers triggered two small avalanches. One of the March 7th avalanches caught one of the backcountry tourers, but they were uninjured. The other avalanche was triggered remotely and broke just below the March 8th accident site.||A full summary of this accident was unavailable. The synopsis given, via CAIC, indicates that a skier triggered and was subsequently caught, carried, and seriously injured by, an avalanche. The skier's partner assisted in digging the skier out of the snow and addressing the injuries as best as possible. The partner then dragged the skier down nearly 600 vertical feet to a trail intersection, where local search and rescue teams were waiting. The skier was then transported to Aspen Valley Hospital via helicopter.

Heavy rain on the mountains adjacent to the southeast part of the town of Ouray produced flash flooding on Oak Creek and Canyon Creek.  The wall of water was six feet deep at the Box Canyon geothermal water plant where sediment got into the water line.  Sediment carried by the  water line was in inch deep at the Ouray Hot Springs.  The Hot Springs had to be closed around 4 PM MDT and remained closed for the rest of that day to clean out the sediment.  Six feet of South Pinecrest Road was washed out, and a culvert under that road was damaged.  Debris up to a foot-and-a-half deep was deposited on other roads.

A flash flood came down Corbett Creek leaving a debris fan several hundred yards long, 300 feet wide and five feet deep.  A house on Whispering Pines Drive sustained extensive damage to the foundation and exterior, with the deck having been ripped off.  Another house on Chipmunk Way had debris up to a half foot deep into the basement and garage, and a deposit of debris up to 2 feet deep on the deck and against the house. A family of hikers on the Dallas Trail became stranded when their parked car was washed away.  Their car was a total loss.  Another car was carried away from a driveway and dropped over a short cliff. A boulder the size of a small car fell onto nearby Highway 550.  County Road 17 was washed out and another nearby private road was washed out in places. The flash flood resulted in Corbett Creek carving out a new channel.  A local official said this was the worst flash flood he had seen in that area since 1991.

Heavy rainfall on the south side of the Uinta Mountains produced widespread flash flooding across a large portion of Uintah County which extended from northwest to southwest of Vernal.  Highway 40 southwest of Vernal was closed for a while due to flood waters across the road. Many other roads in the impacted area were covered extensively with debris, up to four feet deep in places.  A portion of the Red Cloud Loop Road was washed out, with water flowing up to 10 feet deep and 15 feet wide.   Raging water came down the streets of the Flake subdivision west of Maeser.  Five homes had water in their basements and some had water in their garages, although most homes in the Flake subdivision are built up above the road.  There was extensive damage to fences, trees, sheds, equipment, and landscaping in that subdivision.  Debris also filled the sewer lines in the Maeser area.
Rushing water up to 3 feet deep was roaring down normally dry drainages south of Rangely.

Flash flooding in the downtown area of Grand Junction was preceded by rainfall a couple of hours earlier that saturated the ground.  Water over a foot and a half deep flowed down the streets, with pools of water up to three feet deep on some roads.  Storm-drain manhole covers blew off on some streets with water gushing out.  Minor flooding was reported at some downtown businesses on North Avenue and also on Main Street.
Three rockslides occurred in de Beque Canyon following heavy rainfall.  One eastbound lane of I-70 was closed until road crews could remove the rocks and boulders.
Strong outflow winds from thunderstorms blew limbs off trees and also blew the roof off of a business on South 8th Street.
No damage reported.
A six foot wall of water roared down Government Creek which normally runs no deeper than a trickle in August.
Two simultaneous funnel clouds were observed by many eyewitnesses in eastern Archuleta County.

Per the CAIC forecast for the day of the incident, the overall avalanche threat in the area of the incident was rated as Moderate (2/5), with Low (1/5) being the lowest threat and Extreme (5/5) being the highest. The breakdown at different elevation bands gave Moderate (2/5) threats Near and Above treeline, while areas below treeline were rated as Low (1/5). The main avalanche type of concern was Wind Slab, with west through north through to east facing slopes the areas of concern. Likelihood was rated as Possible (2/5), with Unlikely (1/5) the lowest likelihood and Certain (5/5) the highest. The expected size was rated as Small to Large, meaning avalanches could range from mostly harmless outside of unfavorable terrain to large enough to bury, injure, or kill someone. The Avalanche Forecast Discussion for this area highlighted the fact that the avalanche problem was isolated, but reactive when found. You won't find many dangerous wind-loaded slopes, but when you do, there is a good chance you will trigger an avalanche. As for the actual incident avalanche, little data is available from the summary. The incident occurred on an east-facing slope at treeline, where the avalanche threat was rated as Moderate (2/5). Two backcountry skiers were in the area, and had already noticed some sloughing in the snowpack but as it was very unconsolidated and light, had decided to continue to ski. At the top of their second lap down, the slough had consolidated and was moving much faster, catching both skiers on their way down. Skier 1, who wrote the report, was able to escape, but Skier 2 lost a ski in the avalanche was carried all the way down, and ultimately was injured. No information was given as to the severity of the injury. The avalanche was rated as D1.5, or the higher end of a Small avalanche, and was small relative to its path.

Additionally, this event qualified as a hard freeze, as the sensors recorded an average of 6.5 hours at or below 28F, with a maximum of 18 hours and a minimum of 0. The lowest temperature recorded across the Southeast Utah zone, as well as the lowest temperature recorded at the KBDG AWOS in Blanding, UT, was 20F. A total of 9 out of the 11 available temperature sensors in the zone recorded at least 3 hours of temperatures below 32F. The average time below 32F was 8 hours, with a maximum of 13 hours and a minimum of 0 hours. The average duration of temperatures at or below 28F was only 2.5 hours, which does not qualify this event as a hard freeze, however some locations saw up to 9 hours of temperatures at or below 28F. Under clear skies and light winds, temperatures across southeast Utah dropped below 32F again on the night of April 3rd to the 4th. events.cz_name: GORE AND ELK MOUNTAINS/CENTRAL MOUNTAIN VALLEYS
events.event_narrative: A snowboarder was caught and killed in a large avalanche between Vail Pass summit and East Vail. The snowboarder was engulfed by the powder cloud and was carried over 3 cliff bands and swept through numerous small pine trees before being buried about 4 feet deep, about 750 vertical feet down the slope. The other two party members quickly found the boarder but were unable to revive him.

Lightning strikes caused several power outages, including one that affected 3,650 customers in the Durango Mountain Resort area. The outages occurred when lightning struck a power line. The outages lasted from 10 minutes to about 2 hours.
Lightning struck a power supply and left about 550 customers without power for several hours. Electrical crews had to use a backhoe to get at equipment damaged by the strike.
Lightning struck and destroyed a transducer at the Red Canyon Water Treatment Plant.

Lightning struck a home in Vail Valley and ignited a fire within the floor structure and the ceiling cavity. The fire burned through five structural floor joists.  The lightning also blew apart a section of the stone chimney and sent pieces flying up to 20 feet away.

The Vernal CWOP site on the west side of the city of Vernal recorded two wind gusts at or above 58 mph. The first gust, to 58 mph, occurred at 1:20 PM MDT, and the second gust, to 72 mph, occurred at 6:10 PM MDT. These were the only two gusts to reach this strength in the area on this day. No reports of injuries, damages, or fatalities were received.

The peak gust of 59 mph occurred at KCNY ASOS at Canyonlands Airport, near Moab, at 12:39 PM MDT. Gusts across the region ranged from 45 mph up to the peak gust of 59 mph. No reports of injuries, damages, or fatalities were received.

The peak gust to 59 mph occurred at the Bryson Canyon RAWS at 2:48 PM MDT. Gusts across the region ranged from 45 mph up to the peak of 59, with the KCNY ASOS recording a gust to 49 mph, and other RAWS in the region recording gusts to the low to mid 50s mph. No reports of injuries, damages, or fatalities were received.

All the gusts above the 75 mph threshold were recorded at the Colorado Department of Transportation Douglas Pass mesonet station. The peak gust to 83 mph was recorded at 2:29 PM MDT, while another gust to 78 mph occurred at 5:12 PM MDT. Other sites across the zone only saw gusts into the 40s and 50s. However, geography and elevation contribute to this site seeing such high winds. Douglas Pass is a gap oriented north to south with higher terrain to the east and west of the gap. This would act to funnel winds through, with strongest gusts occurring when winds are coming from the south or the north. Winds on this day were southerly, maximizing the funneling effect. No reports of injuries, damages, or fatalities were received.

The Colowyo Fire started in mid to late June due to downed power line near the Colowyo Strip Mine, which is about 19 miles southwest of Craig, Colorado. The fire grew to 585 acres before it was contained a day later in mid to late June. The estimated final cost was $250,000.

The Bridge Creek Fire started in mid June due to a lightning strike on the north side of Navajo Mountain, which is about 55 miles northwest of Page, Arizona. The fire grew to 2,588 acres before it was contained in mid to late July. The estimated final cost was $10 million. This fire is located in San Juan County, Utah near or along the border with WFO SLC.

The Horse Draw Fire started in late June due to a lightning strike 24 miles east of Dinosaur, Colorado. The fire grew to 748 acres before it was contained three days later in late June. The estimated cost to date was $216,022.

The Spencer Fire started in late June due to a human caused incident in which a vehicle fire quickly spread about 2 miles west-southwest of Blue Mountain, Colorado. The fire grew to 237 acres before it was contained 6 hours later on the same day.

The Hilltop Fire started in late June about 7 miles southeast of Rifle. The cause is undetermined. The fire grew to 326 acres before it was contained a couple days later in late June. The estimated cost to date was $430,000. 1 home and 1 RV were lost in the fire.

The Colorado Department of Transportation closed down both lanes of Colorado Highway 145 at mile marker 95 due to a mudslide around 1:35 PM MDT. This closure was lifted later that afternoon, once the road was cleared of mud. No reports of damages, fatalities, or injuries were received other than the temporary road closure.

Flash flooding was reported along Taylor Canyon on the afternoon of June 4h. This flooding eroded a six food embankment along White Rim Road in Canyonlands National Park, and carried sediment all the way to the Green River. Additionally, several washes along Taylor Canyon Road ran and washed out sections of Taylor Canyon Road. No other damages, and no injuries or fatalities, were received.

Flash flooding was observed along Salt Creek down to the confluence with the Dolores River, near the intersection of Salt Creek Road and Colorado Highway 141. A COOP observer nearby reported a pickup truck caught in the flood and floated upright downstream. Additionally, a Colorado Department of Transportation grader was noted leaving the CDOT facility in nearby Gateway and headed toward the area of this flash flooding. No reports of additional damage, or any injuries or fatalities were received.

At approximately 6:20 PM MDT, a severe thunderstorm moved southwest of Chimney Rock National Monument, producing heavy rain and hail. This heavy rain fell on an area of very steep terrain and produced a mud flow and small rock slide across Colorado Highway 151. Aside from the road needing to be cleared, no damage, injuries, or fatalities were reported in association with this debris flow.

This gust was associated with a small thunderstorm that had formed over the Dinosaur National Monument area. This was the only gust recorded in the area, and no reports of damages, injuries, or fatalities were received associated with it.

The Great Divide 2N RAWS recorded a wind gust to 60 mph at approximately 5:46 PM MDT on June 12th. This gust was associated with a passing band of showers and thunderstorms. No reports of damages, injuries, or fatalities were recorded.

At approximately 1:48 PM MDT, the Bryson Canyon RAWS recorded a wind gust to 59 mph. Other gusts recorded across the zone ranged from 45 mph to the peak gust of 59 mph at Bryson Canyon, and occurred throughout the afternoon of the 20th. No reports of injuries, damages, or fatalities were received.

The first was a gust to 78 mph at 11:39 AM MDT, followed by the peak gust to 89 mph at 1:31 PM MDT, and an additional gust to 75 mph at 5:56 PM MDT. Other gusts around the zone were in the upper 40s and 50s mph. The Douglas Pass site is one of the highest sensors in the zone, and is oriented along a north-south axis that does well in wind regimes such as this one, explaining the particularly high wind gusts achieved at this location. No reports of injuries, damages, or fatalities were received associated with this event.

The South Rim Fire started in early July due to multiple lightning strikes 9 miles east of Montrose, Colorado which ignited fires on both the north and south rim of the Black Canyon of the Gunnison National Park. The South Rim Fire became the larger of the two, which grew to 4,232 acres before it was contained in early to mid September. The North Rim Fire was quickly put out one day after it started on July 11th. The north rim of the park was reopened to the public July 30th, while the south rim reopened to the public on August 18th. The estimated cost to date was $15,300,000.

A fire-induced tornado occurred at the Deer Creek Fire near La Sal, Utah on July 12th. The tornado was rated an EF2 with a path of 100 yards wide and winds estimated at 122 mph, lasting approximately 12 minutes. Storm surveys indicated extensive roof damage to a home and several outbuildings were also damaged.
A strong thunderstorm over the Eastern Uinta Mountains produced outflow winds up to 59 mph, which was a measured peak wind gust at the Vernal Regional Airport at 1444 MST.
A peak wind gust of 58 mph occurred at the Rangely Airport at 1535 MST due to a decaying shower with no lightning present.

A mudslide occurred on Highway 133 due to heavy rainfall from a thunderstorm at mile marker 59.5. Radar estimated that 0.7 to 1.4 inches of rain fell within the drainage above Highway 133. The mudslide was reported at 1530 MST.

The KGJT ASOS located the Grand Junction Regional Airport recorded a 2 hour period where visibility was less than 2 miles, with periods of visibility as low as 1/4 mile. During this period, sustained winds of 25-40 mph were recorded, with gusts up to 51 mph. Ongoing construction in and around the airport did contribute to the available dust to blow around, but the extended nature of this event warranted inclusion. No reports of impacts were received.

The KVEL ASOS at Vernal Airport in Vernal, UT recorded sustained winds 25-40 mph, with gusts upward of 60 mph. Thanks to ongoing drought conditions, there was plenty of loose soil and dust to be picked up by strong winds like these, and indeed the KVEL ASOS recorded a half hour period of visibility reduced below 1/2 mile. No reports of impacts due to this dust storm were received.

Training storms off the La Sals resulted in waterfalls off terrain just southeast of Gateway (approx 1900 UTC). No impacts other than inundating basecamp for the Turner Gulch fire, which was set up in a floodplain along the Dolores river, southeast of town (by bridge with USGS gage). Flooding was not associated with the ongoing Turner Gulch Fire to the west of the flood location. Reports associated with this event were provided by fire personnel at the Turner Gulch Basecamp. While the land around the basecamp was inundated, the camp itself was not impacted, and conditions dried out enough that no firefighting apparatus was stuck in the mud. Therefore there were no impacts or damages associated with this event. There were also no injuries or fatalities.

The Grease Fire started in early August due to a lightning strike 12 miles west-southwest of Meeker, Colorado. The fire grew to 1,000 acres before merging into the Lee Fire and acreage was combined for both fires one day later, in which the complex was then just known as the Lee Fire. The end date and time is the moment when the Grease was combined into the Lee Fire. See Lee Fire episode for further information.

The Lee Fire started in early August due to a lightning strike 20 miles southwest of Meeker, Colorado. The Grease Fire grew into the Lee Fire on August 4 and acreage was combined and further known as the Lee Fire. The fire grew to 137,758 acres before it was contained in mid September. The estimated cost to date was $30,106,091. At least five homes and 14 additional structures, such as outbuildings were destroyed by the Lee Fire. The Lee Fire became the fifth largest wildfire in Colorado history. Despite the damage, no injuries or deaths were reported.

Two rock/mud slides were reported on Highway 133, about 10 miles south of Carbondale, between mile-markers 60 and 63. The road was reported as passable but with mud and debris on the road as of approximately 10:20 AM MDT. Reports from the Colorado Department of Transportation. Road was not closed, but did require clean-up. No reports of injuries or fatalities were received.

As of approximately 10:10 AM MDT, two rock slides were reported to have occurred on Highway 82 in Snowmass Canyon. No road closures were reported, and no damages occurred. Road did have to be cleared. No injuries or fatalities were reported.

At approximately 12:15PM MDT, the Rio Blanco Emergency Manager reported a debris flow over County Road 8 between mile-markers 10 and 11. This debris flow was the result of heavy rainfall on the recent Elk RBX burn scar, which was adjacent to the road. Road did need to be cleared, but was already closed to public traffic due to the ongoing Elk RBX fire. No additional damage, or injuries or fatalities were reported.

This incident was reported to the NWS Grand Junction office by the NWS Incident Meteorologist assigned to the Lee Wildfire. Debris flowed across County Road 5 from due to heavy rain on the adjacent Lee burn scar. A tractor trailer attempted to drive through the debris flow and became stuck. The truck was eventually unstuck and the road was cleared. No damages or injuries or fatalities were reported.

This incident was reported to NWS Grand Junction by the NWS Incident Meteorologist deployed to the Lee Wildfire. Water was reported as flowing over Highway 13 adjacent to the Lee Burn Scar, near the incident on County Road 5, and south of the town of Meeker. All of this water drains into the White River, and the gage on the White River below Meeker spiked from roughly 110 cfs to 1660 cfs, with a rise in water height of 3 feet.

At approximately 5:30 PM MDT, the Boulder Service Hydrologist reported a debris flow south of the Lee Burn Scar flowing over Highway 64 between mile-marker 65 and mile-marker 66. This is in the lower Powell Park area. This region is known for debris flows, but this particular event was enhanced by flow off the adjacent burn scar. However, no damages, injuries, or fatalities were reported.

A video of flash flooding within a local area known as Josephine Basin, west of Meeker, was sent to NWS Grand Junction via Facebook. This flash flooding began within the Lee Burn Scar, and washed down over Rio Blanco County Road 33. This flooding was not reported to have caused significant damage, but did prevent residents living along County Road 33 from getting to or from their homes until the water retreated.

At approximately 5:20 PM MDT, heavy rain in the area north of Mexican Hat, UT, resulting in failed culverts and flash flooding. On State Highway 163, the failed culverts and and heavy rain resulted in water over the road, making them impassable until the water receded. Additionally, heavy rain in this region led to water over the road on County Highway 261, in an area of steep switchbacks. While no damage was reported, these roads did become impassable and had to be cleared in the hours after the water receded. No injuries or fatalities were reported.

At approximately 1:18 PM MDT, a report reached NWS Grand Junction that heavy rain over the Lee Burn Scar had triggered a debris flow over Rio Blanco County Road 5 in the same area that had run on August 24th. This time, no vehicles were trapped and no other damage occurred, nor were any injuries or fatalities reported.

Heavy rain on the Lee Burn Scar led to debris flows that filled culverts along Highway 13, particularly at the intersection of Rio Blanco County Road 33. This led to flooding of fields and ranches in the Josephine Basin region, just south and west of Meeker. Some debris was also noted along the side of both County Road 33 and Highway 13.

At approximately 3:20 PM MDT, local law enforcement reported a rockfall between mile-markers 115 and 116 on Highway 141 in Unaweep Canyon, roughly 4 miles east of the town of Gateway. The Turner Gulch burn scar, which is adjacent to this location, experienced some heavy rain prior to this event. This did result in the need for the road to be cleaned, although no reports of the road being closed specifically due to this rockfall were received. Additionally, no reports of damages, injuries, or fatalities were received.

The NWS Incident Meteorologist assigned to the Lee Fire reported this event to NWS Grand Junction. Mud and debris were confirmed to be flowing across Rio Blanco County Road 5 at mile marker 6 and mile marker 12, making the road impassable. As a result, County Road 5 was closed from miles marker 12 to the intersection with Highway 13 for roughly half an hour.

The NWS Incident Meteorologist deployed to the Lee Fire reported this event to NWS Grand Junction. Thunderstorms produced heavy rain over the Lee Burn Scar on the afternoon of August 28th. This in turn resulted in water, mud, and debris flowing over Rio Blanco County Road 5 near mile marker 30, roughly 20 miles west of meeker and on the west side of the Lee Burn Scar. A Flash Flood Warning had been issued for this region with 30 minutes of lead time. No reports of damages, injuries, or fatalities were received. County Road 5 did have to be closed for a short duration to clear the debris.

At approximately 5:47PM MDT the KCEZ ASOS at Cortez-Montezuma County Airport recorded a wind gust to 60 mph, with other nearby gusts recording 45-55 mph. There was a thunderstorm nearby at the time, marking this as a thunderstorm wind gust. No reports of damages, injuries, or fatalities were received in association with this event.

At approximately 4:48 PM MDT, the KEEO ASOS at Meeker Airport recorded a gust to 58 mph in association with a nearby thunderstorm. Other gusts in the area ranged from 45 mph to 55 mph. No reports of damages, fatalities, or injuries were received in association with this event.

The NWS Incident Meteorologist on the Stoner Mesa fire reported snapped trees and uprooted cottonwood trees along Colorado State Route 38 near the Mavreeso Campground. No direct measurement of the winds was recorded, therefore the wind for this entry was estimated. This was the only reported damage, and there were no reports of injuries or fatalities.

The CoCoRaHS reported at Mack 5NW called in a report of a 61 mph wind gust at her location in association with a passing thunderstorm. No reports of injuries, damages, or fatalities were received in association with this event.

At 3:06 PM MDT, NWS Grand Junction received a report from local law enforcement that powerlines had been downed in nearby Fruita, CO in association with a passing severe thunderstorm. Six minutes later, this storm reached the Grand Junction Regional Airport, where the KGJT ASOS recorded a wind gust to 68 mph. No other damages were reported with this event, and no reports of injuries or fatalities were received.

At 4:34 PM MDT, the KRIL ASOS at Rifle - Garfield County Regional Airport recorded a gust to 58 mph, with other gusts nearby in the 50-55 mph range. These gusts were associated with a passing thunderstorm. No reports of damages, injuries, or fatalities were received in association with this event.

An NWS Employee reported power outages across the northern portions of the City of Grand Junction in association with a passing thunderstorm. There was no direct measurement of the winds with this storm, and as such the wind gust is estimated based on the damage done. There were no other damages reported, nor any injuries or fatalities.

At 2:39 PM MDT, the KRIL ASOS at Rifle - Garfield County Regional Airport recorded a wind gust to 58 mph in association with a passing thunderstorm. There were no other recorded gusts with this storm, and no damages, injuries, or fatalities were reported in association with this event.

The Bryson Canyon RAWS station recorded a gust to 60 mph in association with a passing line of thunderstorms. To the south, the KCNY ASOS at Canyonlands Airport recorded a gust to 54 mph in association with this same line. No reports of damages, injuries, or fatalities were reported with this storm.

At 2:30 PM MDT, the mesonet site US-191 at MP 104 Flat Iron recorded a wind gust to 60 mph in association with a passing thunderstorm. Other sensors in the area recorded wind gusts of 45-55 mph in association with the same storm. No reports of damages, injuries, or fatalities were received in association with this storm.

At 5:44 PM MDT, the KRIL ASOS at Rifle - Garfield County Regional Airport recorded a gust to 60 mph. Other sensors in the area at the time recorded wind gusts of 45 mph to 55 mph.
