The second tornado prompted a damage survey conducted by local emergency|management and Navajo Nation emergency management, along with local law enforcement. The data from the survey was relayed to the National Weather Service: storm damage was concentrated on an area centered near 37.33071N / 109.3259W and included; a home completely destroyed, two (2) 800-gallon water barrels were missing, a three-bedroom home was completely destroyed, a sheep corral and barn were destroyed, two (2) horse trailers were damaged, a cow corral, along with damage to three (3) vehicles.

Thunderstorms developed over the Redlands area of Grand Junction late in the afternoon of September 4th, and remained there for 2-3 hours. Impacts began to be noticed around 6:45 PM MDT, with an LSR in the area of 1 ESE Redlands indicating Water out of the banks of nearby wash and running over Redlands Parkway in several areas. Approximately half an hour later, another LSR indicated that water running over the roadway in many areas along South Camp Road in the Redlands (Redlands 1SSE). Debris was also reported as having to be removed from Monument Road (Redlands 3SSE). In addition to the LSR'd events, properties were flooded, normally dry washes were overfilled, and water and debris inundated several roadways in the area. Additionally, social media reports indicated flooding along No Thoroughfare Canyon, Monument Road, and in the Devil's Kitchen area of Colorado National Monument. Once the rain stopped and the storms dissipated, a local spotter provided the total precipitation from this storm, which was a 2.33 inches.

Public reported flash flooding over Archuleta County Road 500/169 Trujillo Road between Arboles and Caracas. There were additional washouts reported near Arboles point, along Trujillo road about 2 miles southeast from the initial LSR location.

National Park Service employees based at Chimney Rock National Monument reported flash flooding on State Route 151 between Pagosa Springs and Arboles. Additionally, washouts and debris were reported in the Chimney Rock National Monument itself, with the LSR reading Upper road and parking lots impassable. Chimney Rock National Monument had to be closed the following day (September 13th, 2025) to clear debris.
National Park Service employees at Arches National Park reported Cache Valley Road had washed out near the lower Delicate Arch viewpoint.
Kane Creek Boulevard/Kane Springs Road and Potash Road reported as impassable due to flooding and mud on the roadways.
Law Enforcement reported standing water on Interstate 70 near Cisco, UT due to heavy rain from passing thunderstorms.

Utah Department of Transportation traffic cameras indicated flooding/ponding of water at the intersection of US Highway 191 and State Route 128, north of the town of Moab. This was due primarily to heavy rainfall on already saturate soils. Impacts were minimal and once the rain stopped, the roadway cleared.

Public reported flooding across State Highway 139 south of Douglas Pass due to several rounds of heavy rain training over the steep and saturated terrain. No reports of road closures or damages to the roadway.

A trained spotter reported street flooding at the intersection of State Route 340 and Rimrock Drive, near the west entrance to Colorado National Monument. No reports of road closures or damages due to this flooding were received.
Law Enforcement reported a debris flow that closed County Road 5 due to heavy rain on the recent Lee Burn Scar.
Law Enforcement reported mud and debris on State Route 8 due to heavy rain on the recent Elk RBX Burn Scar. No reports of damages, injuries, or fatalities, just clearing of the roadway.

Heavy rain due to the remnants of Tropical Storm Priscilla falling between the evening of October 9th and October 11th, resulted in flooding along Vallecito Creek, which began rising around midnight on October 11th. Vallecito Creek crested at 1245 MST on October 11 to 5.99 feet and 7100 cfs, which is a new record historical peak, beating the previous record of 5.98 feet set on September 6 of 1970. The flood wave routed through the system through the evening of October 11th with streamflows dropping about 2 feet from the peak around 2200 on October 11th. There were 7 road closures, 600 to 700 residences were evacuated in Vallecito and there were 11 high water rescues in addition to threatened bridges. Debris was seen moving down the river including trees and objects from people's homes including a hot tub. Vallecito Creek remained elevated with a second crest of 4.38 feet around 800 MST on October 14 in response to another period of locally heavy rain and increased rates on October 13. The second flood wave routed through the system by 300 MST on October 16, before subsiding below bankfull levels. This second wave carved out a completely new channel moving at 3000 cfs.

Significant rainfall fell across the San Juan River Basin between the evening of October 9 and October 11 due to the remnants of Tropical Storm Priscilla. This resulted in major flooding along the San Juan River in Pagosa Springs. Action stage of 9.48 feet was exceeded on October 11 at 1100 MST. The San Juan River crested at major flood stage on October 11 at 1600 MST at 12.66 feet and 8270 cfs. The San Juan River then fell to near action stage on October 12 at 1000 MST. Four places were impacted in Archuleta County which were mostly rural. Most of the damage reported were dirt roads washed out and minor flooding to residents where the river exceeded its banks. There were numerous power outages and a water main broke in Pagosa Springs which was repaired on October 12. Preliminary estimates of $5 million to repair man-made white water rapids for kayaking and recreation along the San Juan River in Pagosa Springs and $2 million estimated to repair the bike path along the San Juan River in Pagosa Springs.

The San Juan River reached a second crest to major flood stage that was even higher than the first in response to additional significant rainfall and locally heavier rates on October 13. This heavy rainfall was due to the remnants of Tropical Storm Raymond on top of already saturated ground from the previous surge from Tropical Storm Priscilla. The San Juan River climbed back to action stage on October 13 at 1300 MST at 9.48 feet. The second crest reached major flood stage on October 14 at 300 MST at 12.88 feet. The San Juan River then fell below action stage on October 15 at 700 MST.
Rock falls occurred along Highway 550 near the Red Mountain Pass snowshed which is between mile markers 87 and 88, due to significant rainfall reported around 1000 MST on October 11.
Significant rainfall resulted in a rockslide on Highway 145 near Norwood Hill between 900 and 930 MST. Deputies arrived on site by 1030 MST and the rock debris was cleared by 1100 MST.

Heavy rain resulted in a rockslide on Highway 45 at mile marker 64.5, about 1 mile north of the Ophir turns between 0900 and 0930 MST. A boulder the size of a small sedan fell on Highway 145, blocking the road. Lanes were reopened by 1030 MST.
Heavy rain caused mud and rockslides on Frying Pan Road in Pitkin County. Road closed at 511 MST and was reopened by 623 MST.

Radar indicated heavy rain between 0300 and 0400 MST. This heavy rain caused multiple mudslides to occur around 0400 MST between Carbondale and Redstone along Highway 133 centered around mile marker 55.7. Another one occurred at mile marker 53 within this similar timeframe. One vehicle was stuck in the mudslide but not buried. No indication of how deep or wide the slide was but clean up took longer than usual due to the stuck vehicle. Road reopened in both directions at 0917 MST.
Heavy rain resulted in a rock slide on Douglas Pass along Highway 139 at mile marker 33, 29 miles north of Loma, Colorado. Highway 139 closed at 531 MST.
Heavy rain resulted in a rockslide on County Road 250 around 430 MST.

The Piedra River had a rapid rise in levels throughout the morning and afternoon of October 11th due to abundant rainfall starting on October 10th. It first crested to a preliminary level of 5.86 ft around midnight 10/12.  A second crest occurred to a preliminary level of 7.26 ft on 10/14 around 1300 MST. This set a new record, beating the previous crest record of 6.4 ft which was set back on 9/6/1970. Most issues were adjacent to the 151 corridor north of Arboles where numerous drives were under water, one garage had some water in it. Forest Service Rd 613 did have some inundation but most bridges had several feet of clearance. USFS 613 which is parallel to the river did have water in some areas.

The Derby Fire started in mid August due to a lightning strike 13.5 miles north of Dotsero, Colorado. The fire grew to 5,453 acres spreading across Eagle and Garfield counties. While major suppression efforts ended in October and significant fire activity ceased, the remaining 5 percent was in an inaccessible area with pockets of interior smoke. It was officially 100 percent contained by mid December. The estimated cost was $23,860,000.

At the beginning of the month of December the US Drought Monitor analyzed an area of Extreme (D3) Drought in Colorado Zone 008 - Central Colorado River Basin. This area comprised roughly 25% of the zone, with the remainder under Severe (D2) Drought conditions. As of the 12/24 Drought Monitor update, Exceptional (D4) Drought developed in the zone, covering roughly 5% of the zone, with 20% now under Extreme (D3) Drought conditions, and the remaining 75% still under Severe (D2) Drought conditions. With the 12/31 update, the area of Exceptional (D4) Drought area remained at 5% coverage, but the area of Exception (D4) Drought expanded to cover 40% of the zone. The remaining 55% of the zone was under Severe (D2) Drought.

events.event_narrative: To summarize the write up provided by the Colorado Avalanche Information Center (CAIC) regarding this incident: The area of the incident is known locally as King Arthur's/Timber Falls (39.628, -106.308). 1 backcountry tourer caught and partially buried, injured. Skier triggered avalanched rated as R2 and D2, meaning it was small relative to it's path but was large enough to catch, injure or kill a person. Avalanche was below treelline and on an east facing slope. CAIC had rated the avalanche danger in that area on that day a 2/5 or moderate, mainly at or above treeline, with danger ranged 1/5 or low below treeline. North through east facing slopes rated most dangerous. 2 skiers triggered the avalanche, with only one being caught and pinned against a tree, suffering cuts and abrasions. With assistance from the other skier, who was able to avoid the avalanche, the trapped skier was freed and both were able to leave the site of the avalanche.

On the accident day, the avalanche danger in the area was rated 3/5 - Considerable at all levels, below, near, and above treeline. Avalanche danger was rated on all aspects, with large to very large avalanches likely west through north to east aspects, and small avalanches possible on southwest through southeast aspects. Avalanche discussion indicated that recent avalanches in the area had been large enough to bury, injure, or kill a person, and could be triggered remotely, from a distance or below, and could travel long distances. The accident group consisted of three backcountry tourers, 1 split board rider and 2 skiers, and the intention was to ski a southwest slope from a sub-peak south of Bonita Peak into Minnehaha Basin (37.893, -107.625). Before ascending toward their destination, they stomped on several areas of drifted snow with no reaction. South slopes noted to have shallow snowpack. Rider 1 descended first and made two ski cuts with no reactivity, then started down the slope. A number of turns into Rider 1's descent the avalanche broke and the Rider was caught, tumbling end over end down the rocky path. Rider 1 came to a stop in a standing position at the bottom of the path, buried from the waist down. A second avalanche, triggered by Skier 1 in the hangfire, struck Rider 1 and pushed them further downhill, leaving them in a seated position. Skier 1, who triggered this avalanche, was also caught and carried, bouncing over rocks and left with their legs buried and an injured arm. Rider 1 was able to self-extricate and moved to Skier 1 to extricate them. Skier 2 chose to descend the way they had ascended, and all met and returned to the trailhead. The larger of the two avalanches was rated R2/D2, meaning it was small relative to its path but was large enough to catch, bury, injure, or kill a person. The smaller avalanche was rated R1/D1, meaning it was very small relative to its path and was small enough to be mostly harmless.

On the accident day, the avalanche danger in the area in question was rated 3/5 - Considerable for areas near and above treeline. Below treeline, avlanche danger was rated 2/5 or moderate. A Special Avalache Advisory was in effect due to recent snow and strong winds forming thick, cohesive slabs over an unusually weak and shallow snowpack. Slopes with wind drifted snow were indicated as most dangerous, with deep (2-3 feet) buried weak layers giving little warning before breaking into an avlanche. Avalanches of small to large size were likely at all levels on aspects northwest through north to east, and likely near or above treeline on aspects south through southeast. The accident group consisted of 4 skiers, who had spent most of the day successfully skiing east facing slopes. For the last run of the day, the group chose a northeast-facing slope south of the Hahns Peak Lake Dam (40.830, -106.986). Skier 1 did ski cuts that were unreactive, and successfully skied the skier's left side of the slope. Skier 2 began their run and after two turns the avalanche broke. Skier two was knocked off their feet and caught, eventually tumbling before being slammed against a tree. They were headfirst on their back, with snow up to their chin, but were able to clear their mouth and wave for help. One of the remaining members of the group were able to extricate Skier 2 and help them down, under their own power but with assistance. Unknown extent of injuries. Avalanche had a 2 foot fracture line, was 30 feet wide and ran 100 feet. Avalanche occurred below treeline on a northeast-facing slope, and was rated R2/D2, meaning it was small relative to its path but large enough to catch, carry, bury, injure, or kill a person.

events.cz_name: GORE AND ELK MOUNTAINS/CENTRAL MOUNTAIN VALLEYS
events.event_narrative: All information paraphrased from the Colorado Avalanche Information Center report on the incidence. The fatal avalanche was triggered by a solo backcountry skier in an area known locally as Boss Basin, in the area of Vail Pass, CO. Boss Basin is comprised of a series of northeast-facing slopes that are low-angled at the top, descending into steeper slopes below, ending at a flat bench. Conditions in the Vail Pass area on the accident day were rated by the Colorado Avalanche Information Center at Moderate (3/5) near and above treeline, with a Considerable (2/5) rating below treeline. The main concern was listed as Persistent Slab Avalanches, favoring slopes northwest through north to northeast facing at all elevation bands. The likelihood was listed as Likely, and size expected listed as Large to Very Large (up to D3), meaning these avalanches would be capable of burying, injuring, or killing a person as well as potential bury cars and break trees.  The avalanche forecast also included wording stating that humans could easily trigger avalanches where [they] find more than about 10 inches of snow, that avalanches that break on buried weak layers would be difficult to survive, and that remote triggering of avalanches would be possible. The backcountry skier that triggered the fatal avalanche, referred from here on as Skier 1, started the day at approximately 7AM local time in the Vail Pass Winter Recreation Area. Skier 1 used a snowmobile to access various terrain through the morning before heading toward Boss Basin around 1:15 PM local time, parking his snowmobile at the top of a nearby ridge. Skier 1 successfully made one descent and climbed back up the slope for a second. On the second descent, Skier 1 triggered the avalanche and was caught and buried near the toe of the avalanche with only the tip of one ski visible. As Skier 1 was alone, no rescue action was taken until family members noticed they were overdue at approximately 11:30 PM local time that evening. Members of Summit County Rescue Group searched through the night, finding the accident location by 6:00 AM local time the next morning. Two rescuers and a search dog were at the avalanche location by 8:00 AM, and the dog quickly alerted on an area of interest. In this location, the rescuers located Skier 1, now deceased, with their head buried approximately 1 foot below the snow surface. Skier 1 was dug out and eventually removed from the location by helicopter.

At the beginning of the month of April, the US Drought Monitor indicated approximately 70% of Colorado Zone 001 - Lower Yampa River Basin was under Exceptional (D4) Drought, with the remaining 25% under Extreme (D3) Drought. These conditions remained unchanged through the end of the month. While no direct impacts from the drought were yet observed, increasing unease among those living and working in this zone has been noted. People are becoming increasingly concerned about water availability through the summer, and what the ongoing drought might mean for summer wildfires. There is also concern over drinking water availability and sourcing. With the lack of snowmelt, water quality is poorer than in typical years. The city of Rangely also has specific concerns regarding water flow rates and level, as they draw water directly from the White River, and if water levels are too low and flow too weak, it becomes impossible to draw water reliably.

There's also concern over water availability through the summer for irrigation and home use. Some local HOAs are estimating water will no longer be available for home use or irrigation by August. Drinking water providers in the Valley are also concerned over water quality. Some source water from the Grand Mesa snowmelt, which has a higher water quality than water sourced from the Colorado River. At this rate, the Grand Mesa snowpack is in such poor shape that most water providers expect to have to use river water to provide drinking water. There's also concern about being able to draw from the Colorado River at all due to low flow and low water levels. Drawing from the river also has water rights concerns, as much of the water through the Colorado River in the Grand Valley is already allocated to areas downstream.

events.cz_name: GORE AND ELK MOUNTAINS/CENTRAL MOUNTAIN VALLEYS
events.event_narrative: A lone backcountry skier was caught and killed in an avalanche in the Richmond Ridge area, just south of Aspen Mountain. Sometime between 1 and 3 pm the victim exited the ski resort through a backcountry gate. Since he was traveling alone, the exact time of the incident is unknown. The victim was carried about 200 vertical feet down the slope before being buried in a group of trees.

Sometime during the afternoon, a 36 year old male snowboarder was caught and killed in an avalanche approximately 2 miles northwest of Crested Butte. The soft slab avalanche occurred in an area known as Happy Chutes. The avalanche ran about 1,500 vertical feet, carrying the victim through a dense grove of trees, over a 20 to 30 foot cliff, then down a tight gully and finally to a stand of small trees. The victim was found about a week later under 3 to 4 feet of snow.

events.cz_name: GORE AND ELK MOUNTAINS/CENTRAL MOUNTAIN VALLEYS
events.event_narrative: A party of two snowboarders and one skier were hiking up a slope near Eiseman Hut in the Gore Range when they were caught and buried in an avalanche.  They all came to rest fairly quickly after being carried about 20 vertical feet.  All three were completely buried; the skier and one snowboarder under 1 to 3 feet of snow, while the other snowboarder was under 6 to 7 feet of snow.  The skier was able to dig himself out of the snow after 1 hour and 20 minutes.  The skier then dug out his partners who had been buried under the snow for up to 2 hours and 15 minutes.  All three activated their AvaLungs after they were buried by the snow, and this safety equipment was instrumental in saving their lives.  The three backcountry travelers suffered only minor injuries, though some of their equipment was damaged.

A Grand Junction home owner in the Redlands area of the city was burning a brush pile when the fire got out of control due to strong winds that developed.  The wildfire burned through 40 acres of residential and open space, forcing the evacuation of 20 homes in the Redlands area of Grand Junction. One firefighter attending to the fire sustained minor burns to his face.  Some monitoring gauges and plastic coverings on the outside of one of the fire engines were melted as the fire roared across Highway 340.  The exterior wall of one house was charred, and landscaping was destroyed on several other properties.

A campfire that was started on an island near the confluence of the Colorado and Gunnison rivers burned out of control when strong winds blew across the Grand Valley during the afternoon and evening hours. Around 6:30 pm, the wildfire jumped the Colorado River moving across a bike path and railroad tracks near the southbound off-ramp of the Riverside Parkway. The fire moved into a salvage yard and burned down a building used for office space and storage. Mobile home residents near Riverside Parkway were evacuated for about 3 hours.

A party of skiers triggered an avalanche while skiing in Bear Creek, near the Telluride ski area. The avalanche carried one skier 1400 vertical feet over several cliff bands, to the valley floor. His entire body was buried except for one hand. He was rescued about 7 minutes later by other members in his party, and was carried out by the Telluride Helitrax and Telluride Ski Patrol. The victim suffered multible broken bones and was taken to St. Mary's Hospital in Grand Junction.

Layers of weak and unstable snow followed by sustained, heavy snowfall, created avalanche prone conditions that gave way to a snowmobile induced avalanche during the afternoon hours of January 4. Three snowmobilers were riding up a snow-covered hill about six miles south of the Marapos Creek trailhead in Rio Blanco county south of Hamilton, when the avalanche occurred and buried one of the snowmobilers head first into the snow. The two other snowmobilers recovered the victim who was unconscious at the time, but regained consciousness shortly thereafter. He was taken to Memorial Hospital in Craig and then to Aurora Hospital.  The victim suffered some pulmonary problems from the snowmobile exhaust that filled his lungs with carbon monoxide while he was trapped underneath the snow.

NWS employees and trained spotters reported large hail across a significant swath of the Grand Valley, from the Redlands area to the downtown Grand Junction area.  At least 800 vehicles were damaged, including vehicles parked outside at six vehicle dealerships.

events.event_narrative: A series of mudslides at the base of Buttermilk Ski Area near Aspen destroyed a thousand gallon oil storage tank and heavily damaged a ski company maintenance building and the equipment inside the building.  The mudslides carried a large number of trees, brush, and rocks, and created a gash on the side of the mountain 50 feet wide and 30 feet deep.

Four men were golfing on the seventh green at the Cedar Ridges Golf Course in Rangely when a tree 15 to 20 yards away was struck by lightning.  The charge from the lightning bolt traveled from the tree through the ground and struck the four golfers, blowing the golf clubs out of their hands and leaving them stunned for a period of time.  They heard popping noises on the tops of their heads as the charge exited through their caps.  One of the golfers felt like the hair on his head was on fire.  The tree struck by lightning was split open and a large amount of bark was blown off.  Information in this report was provided by one of the lightning strike victims.

Strong thunderstorm winds blew down some old trees and broke off large branches from other trees throughout the town of Bluff.

A rockslide occurred in De Beque Canyon that was likely induced by recent rainfall.  Boulders up to five feet in diameter came crashing down onto Interstate 70.  A pickup truck with two occupants was partially crushed by one of the large boulders.  Both occupants survived.

Heavy rainfall resulted in a flash flood with a large amount of mud that flowed across Highway 133.  When the flooding stopped, it left a deposit of mud on the Highway up to 4 feet deep.  The highway was opened to traffic within two hours after the flash flooding ended.

Heavy rainfall caused two new culverts to fill up with debris under a bridge spanning Pack Creek and caused water to flow over the top of the new US Forest Service bridge.  The bridge was damaged and a gorge was formed on the other side of the bridge.

The Grand Junction Regional Airport ASOS reported wind gusts up to 54 mph during the afternoon hours. A local Grand Junction resident lost some roof shingles due to the strong wind gusts, and a former NWS employee reported a 6 foot wooden yard fence being blown down.
A funnel cloud was observed and photographed seven miles northwest of Craig.
A volunteer NWS storm spotter observed large hail mostly over open country.  About half of the Rye crop was damaged.
Hail up to one inch in diameter fell in the town of Maybell.  Gardens were damaged.
Hail up to one inch in diameter completely covered the ground like a layer of snow.
Nickel-size hail pummeled the town of Maybell.  Gardens that were struck by hail earlier in the day were ravaged even further.
Hail up to golf ball size pummeled the Randlett area, damaging crops and gardens.
A funnel cloud was observed from a resident who lives near Little Park Road.
Street flooding was encountered by persons traveling in the vicinity of Orchard Avenue and 29.5 Road.
Heavy rainfall totaling 0.82 of an inch fell within about an hour resulting in minor street flooding.

Heavy rainfall resulted in minor flooding in many areas within the Grand Junction metropolitan area.  Street flooding occurred along North Avenue between 4th and 7th Streets where a manhole cover was blown out, along 7th Street between North Avenue and Orchard Avenue, and on Patterson Road between 12th and 15th Streets.  Flood waters also seeped into the Doubletree Hotel where some water damage occurred.

Heavy rainfall resulted in a mudslide next to I-70 at Exit 42.  The heavy rainfall also caused the fall of several large boulders onto the westbound lanes of I-70 near mile marker 43.   The boulders, which weighed up to a thousand pounds, closed the westbound lanes of I-70 for about an hour until they were all removed.
Heavy rainfall caused street flooding in the southern part of the town of Delta, including the area around 12th and Main Street.
Nickel-size hail damaged gardens and stripped many leaves off trees in the northeast part of Grand Junction.

A microburst traversed a section of the town of Montrose, breaking off numerous large branches and snapping off some trees.  Loose objects such as picnic tables, chairs, and barbecue grills were blown over or tossed around.  It took three days for the City of Montrose to clean up all of the debris on sidewalks and streets.
Lightning struck an oil battery, heavily damaging two large oil tanks and other equipment.
Golf ball size hail struck an area of US Highway 40 southeast of Jensen.  Some vehicles and camper trailers sustained damage.

Heavy rainfall in some areas of Grand Junction resulted in minor street flooding on North Avenue, in Clifton, and in the Redlands.  A spotter in the Redlands area of Grand Junction reported 0.56 of an inch of rain within 15 minutes.
A dust devil traveled directly into an anemometer which measured a peak wind gust of 66 mph.  Unsecured items were blown over and tossed about.
Strong thunderstorm outflow winds blew down and tossed unsecured property.
Strong thunderstorm outflow winds blew down a number of items at a volunteer spotter's residence.
Lightning struck the South Routt Elementary School and started the building on fire.  The fire and related damage were confined to the gymnasium.
Heavy rainfall resulted in minor street and road flooding.  A NWS employee in the impacted area measured 0.75 of an inch of rain within 35 minutes.
A half inch of rain fell within 10 minutes and resulted in some minor flooding.
Minimum temperatures dropped to between 24 and 29 degrees across the area. This affected many local fruit growers that lost early budding fruit.

Strong southerly surface winds blew a large tree branch down on top of a power transformer.  The branch severed a local power line and destroyed the transformer, causing a large power outage in the Redlands area of the Grand Valley.  Additionally, several radio stations in other areas of Grand Junction went off the air due to power outages.  Although measured wind gusts only reached 54 mph in the Grand Valley, it is estimated that there were some stronger gusts where wind measurements were not available.
Snowfall of 2 to 5 inches occurred across the area with some locally higher amounts, including 8 inches in the town of Edwards.

Flash flood waters flowed across Rio Blanco County Road 5 in several places with water over a foot deep in some spots.  A large mudslide came down across the road near mile marker 18.  It took two days to move mud and debris off and away from the road and to make repairs.  Additionally, major soil erosion was reported on some privately owned ranch and farmland in the basin.
Golf ball sized hail struck the town of Rangely.  Minor damage was reported, including shingle damage, dents in cars and a few broken windows.
Hail up to 1.25 inches in diameter pummeled a forested area southeast of Steamboat Lake.

A tornado was observed by many people in the Rangely area and also photographed by a couple of individuals.  The tornado remained over open country during its lifespan.  The tornado track location is an estimate based on triangulation of eyewitness reports.
A funnel cloud was observed by many individuals in the Craig area.  The funnel cloud was also photographed.
Strong outflow winds ahead of a strong thunderstorm blew away and threw down unsecured items in the Pelican Lake area.

Heavy rainfall resulted in flash flooding in the Randlett area.  Fast flowing water from 1 to 3 feet deep washed out several driveways and cut a deep gully across a road that branches off of 7500 East.  Many agricultural fields were flooded, inundating irrigation sprinkler systems.

Golfball size hail struck the Naples area.  Gardens and crops were decimated.  Cars were dented and windows broken.  Many houses and businesses incurred damage to siding and roofs, as well as broken windows.
Fast moving hailstones up to the size of ping pong balls broke windows, dented vehicles, and damaged siding on residences.
Golfball sized hailstones dented vehicles and broke windshields and headlights traveling along highway 191 in the eastern Uinta Mountains.

A tornado was observed by a number of people in the Pelican Lake area.  The tornado was first seen as it came up over a hill just west of Pelican Lake.  The tornado then traveled across Pelican Lake and turned white as it pick up water off the lake.  On the east shore of the lake, the tornado tore up some trees and flipped over a trailer used for living quarters at a man camp.  Nobody was in the trailer at the time of the event.

A tornado tracked through a small section of Vernal, mostly staying between houses.  A number of trees had large limbs broken off and some minor damage occurred to sheds.  The tornado was seen by many area residents and photographed by at least three persons.
Thunderstorm outflow winds up to 60 mph blew across Canyonlands Airport late in the evening.
A microburst from a dry thunderstorm blew a trampoline about a hundred feet and knocked over some cottonwood trees.   Other unsecured objects were blown away.
Heavy rainfall produced street flooding along 400 North in Moab.  A nearby spotter measured 0.75 of an inch of rain in less than 30 minutes.

Thunderstorms produced heavy rainfall that brought a wall of water 5 to 7 feet deep down Kane Creek which inundated a low water crossing of Kane Creek Road and washed away three newer model SUVs.  All three vehicles were destroyed.  All 17 tourists, which included 9 children, abandoned their vehicles just seconds prior to the flash flood arrival.  Eventually, the entire valley filled up with water.  The situation was recorded on videotape by one of the survivors.  Several sheriffs deputies who were enroute to rescue the tourists became stranded near Hoorah Pass by a subsequent mudslide.  Two helicopters from Salt Lake City arrived to the area later and were used to rescue the tourists and sheriffs deputies.

Thunderstorms produced heavy rainfall that produced flash flooding off of higher surrounding terrain into the Spanish Valley area.  Runoff water one to two feet foot deep was flowing rapidly across Highway 191 as a UHP vehicle traveling between mile markers 115 and 116 was washed off the highway.  The highway was damaged in places.

Thunderstorms produced heavy rainfall that produced flash flooding off of higher surrounding terrain into the Moab and Spanish Valley areas.  Water one to two feet deep flowed rapidly across Highway 191 in the Spanish Valley and closed the highway.  Five condos in the Rim Village area had several inches of muddy water seeping into the residences.  Twelve people were stranded by falsh flood waters up Millcreek Canyon near Moab and had to be rescued.

Thunderstorms produced heavy rainfall that resulted in flash flooding across Hastings Road, a county road in Grand County that parallels the Green River.  A large amount of mud and debris covered the road and trapped about twenty campers on the north end of the road until heavy equipment cleared the road late the next day.  A man riding a horse was sent into the river when the bank washed out underneath the horse.  The man was able to swim out of the river, though the horse did not survive.

A thunderstorm produced heavy rainfall near Naturita that produced a flash flood up to three feet deep across Highway 141 west of Naturita.  The most intense flash flooding occurred at the bottom on Calamity Hill on Highway 141.  The highway was closed and road crews were needed to clean debris off the highway.  Additionally, minor flooding was reported on nearby CC Road.

Lightning struck a power substation on the north side of Montrose during the early morning hours, causing minor damage  This caused the electrical power to be down for nearly 1400 residences in northern Montrose County north of the town of Montrose for about 90 minutes.

events.cz_name: GORE AND ELK MOUNTAINS/CENTRAL MOUNTAIN VALLEYS
events.event_narrative: A snowboarder was assumed to have exited Vail Ski Area in Blue Sky Basin, where he proceeded toward the Miller Cliffs on Battle Mountain. While attempting to snowboard outside of ski area boundaries, he triggered 2 small avalanches that came together and carried him roughly 100 feet downhill. He was carried into a stand of trees where he was partially buried head-first and suffocated under 3 feet of snow. The snowboarder was alone and was not recovered until nearly a week later on January 14. Therefore, the time of this accident is estimated.

On the northwest side of Animas Mountain within the Durango city limits, an avalanche roared into a house. The homeowners were about to move into the 15 year old home within the following 2 weeks. Snow blasted through an exterior wall and blew loose drywall onto an interior wall. One bedroom was completely filled with snow, and the home suffered severe structural damage. The avalanche ran about 600 vertical feet with a 150 foot wide path. The damaged home was discovered Sunday, January 24, but the actual time of the avalanche is unknown.

events.cz_name: GORE AND ELK MOUNTAINS/CENTRAL MOUNTAIN VALLEYS
events.event_narrative: A skier triggered an avalanche at the 10,500 foor level in the Mushroom Bowl area near Vail Ski Area. The avalanche path was about 80 feet wide and ran about 650 vertical feet. The skier was caught in the avalanche and partially buried, sustaining minor injuries.  Two other skiers rescued the victim and the Vail Ski Patrol later responded to the incident.

events.cz_name: GORE AND ELK MOUNTAINS/CENTRAL MOUNTAIN VALLEYS
events.event_narrative: Four experienced backcountry skiers headed out-of-bounds and toward Old Man's Bowl just outside of the East Vail area. One of the skiers attempted to ski down the bowl and made a ski cut below the ridgeline heading towards the tree band which separates two portions of East Marvin's. He triggered a small soft slab avalanche  which ran about 200 vertical feet onto a bench. The skier then skied onto and below the bench and triggered a second soft slab avalanche that was about 100 feet wide and ran 400 vertical feet. The skier attempted to ski out to the side and out of the way of the debris flow. While looking over his shoulder he lost his balance, fell, and was caught in the debris and washed down the slope. The skier was buried with his head just below the snow surface.  The other skiers in the group were able to dig him out of the snow. The buried skier sustained a broken arm and several cuts and bruises to his head and limbs.

Seven back-country skiers ventured out on a hut trip near the Ridgeway Hut in the northern San Juan Mountains when two of the skiers were caught in an avalanche. Nearby observations indicated anywhere from 10 to 16 inches of fresh snow had fallen in the 6 days leading up to the event. The skiers were attempting their second run of the day when they decided to split into two groups. One of the skiers in the second group triggered the slide which then carried two of the skiers about 400 feet downhill. One skier was completely buried under 1 to 2 feet of snow, while the other skier was thrown into a large tree. Other party members carrying rescue equipment immediately began searching for the caught skiers. Both skiers were dug out of the snow and brought to the hospital in Montrose by rescue helicopter. The buried skier did not survive, while the other skier suffered multiple traumatic injuries, including a dislocated hip.

events.cz_name: GORE AND ELK MOUNTAINS/CENTRAL MOUNTAIN VALLEYS
events.event_narrative: A group of four back-country skiers were skinning up Mt. Yeckel to attempt their second run for the day, when the lead skier triggered an avalanche. The avalanche carried the first skier 100 feet downhill, where he then hit a tree. The second of the four skiers was also carried downhill but remained on top of the snow surface. The remaining two skiers were able to stay out of the avalanche path. The uninjured skiers contacted Mountain Rescue Aspen, who attended to the injured skier around 3:00 am the next morning. He was flown out by helicopter about 3 hours later and was diagnosed with a broken lower leg.

events.cz_name: GORE AND ELK MOUNTAINS/CENTRAL MOUNTAIN VALLEYS
events.event_narrative: In the week leading up to the date of the accident, Aspen Mountain, which is the closest observing site, reported up to 35 inches of new snowfall. Weak layers underneath the fresh snow created a very unstable snowpack, which lead to the deadly avalanche. A group of 6 people were staying at the Lindley Hut near Ashcroft, and on the day of the accident, 3 people in the group ventured out to ski some of the lower slopes near the hut. The skiers were skinning up a slope about a quarter mile east of the hut, when the first skier triggered a slide that carried him 150 feet downhill and buried him underneath 3 feet of snow in a dense stand of trees. The two other skiers did not witness the initial trigger of the slide, but began to search for the victim after seeing what happened. They contacted Mountain Rescue Aspen who were flown into the site the next morning and eventually found the victim near the toe of the avalanche debris.

events.cz_name: GORE AND ELK MOUNTAINS/CENTRAL MOUNTAIN VALLEYS
events.event_narrative: On the afternoon of February 26th, a group of four back-country skiers exited the Aspen Mountain Ski Area boundaries and entered into Ophir Gulch. Two of the skiers in the group were on the steeper part of the terrain when an avalanche was triggered by one of them. The other skier was below digging a pit when the avalanche began and was carried a short distance by the slide before he was able to grab hold of a tree and avoid being swept further downhill. The other skier, who initially triggered the slide, was carried 500 vertical feet and was buried on the uphill side of a tree. The buried skier was quickly found and attended to by his partners, but the rescue required the assistance of nine Aspen Mountain Ski Patrol members. The victim who sustained serious chest and neck injuries was brought to an ambulance by 8:40 pm that evening.

One male snowmobiler was ascending a slope near Cliff Lake Overlook in the Flat Tops Wilderness Area when he triggered an avalanche. The rider fell off of his machine near the top of the slope, which triggered the slide. He and his machine were carried about 100 feet downhill, but he was able to ride the avalanche in a sitting position and was only partially buried.  The victim did not sustain any serious injuries.

Snowfall amounts of 15 to 17 inches were reported on the northern side of the San Juan mountains just prior to the date of this event, which contributed to unstable snow conditions. A group of 8 back-country skiers headed into the mountains northwest of Silverton for an advanced back-country skiing course. After ascending the slope, the first skier in the group skied down and stopped in a safe patch of trees to wait for the others. The next 5 skiers descended one at a time about 1,000 feet downhill and stopped to wait for the others. The seventh skier descended and fell into a small concavity which released the slide that propagated out in both directions. Only the first and seventh skier were caught and carried in the avalanche, but were both able to recover with no injuries. None of the other skiers were affected.

A series of winter storms in March brought several feet of snow to the San Juan Mountains, including the storm leading up to this event which deposited 21 inches of new snowfall at the nearest observation site. The date of this event was the warmest day of the season to date with strong southerly winds of 20 to 30 mph with gusts to around 60 mph. All of these factors combined to produce what was believed to be a natural avalanche near Baldy Peak. A very experienced back-country traveler and certified alpine mountain guide with professional avalanche training headed out to attempt a remote ice climb on the northeast side of Baldy Peak when she was caught in the avalanche. Because she was traveling alone, many of the details of this event are unknown or estimated. The following day a search and rescue team found the avalanche site along with some of the climber's equipment and her dog, but were unsuccessful in finding the climber. They returned the following day with a larger team and eventually found the body of the missing climber buried under 5 to 6 feet of snow and debris.

Around 1:00 pm on March 17th, two cross country skiers attempted to ski the Thunderbird area on the west side of the Grand Mesa. The skiers were passing through a clearing when a wall of snow above them collapsed. They were both carried an estimated 300 to 800 feet down slope. One of the skiers was dragged into several trees and seriously injured. The second skier was able to contact the Sheriff's Department, who dispatched a search and rescue team that eventually airlifted them to St. Mary's Hospital where the injured skier was put into the intensive care unit. The injured skier suffered two broken legs from the accident.

A snowmobiler with a sled got stuck in flats below a mountain slope near Irwin Lodge. A second snowmobiler drove just above the stuck snowmobiler and triggered three separate avalanches. One of the avalanches came down onto the stuck snowmobiler. His sled rolled on top of him and he was partially buried with his head and hand just above the snow.  The path of that avalanche was 400 vertical feet and was 80 feet wide.  No significant injuries or damage were reported.  The time of the avalanche is an estimate.

Two snowboarders rode down the northwest face of a mountain about four miles northeast of Silverton. The first rider ski cut the top of the open face above the trees, and then rode down 100 vertical feet. The second snowboarder began riding down the slope and triggered an avalanched that started with an upper face fracture of 3 feet deep and 50 feet wide. The first snowboarder waiting below could not escape the slide path and pinned himself on the uphill side of a tree. The slide moved through his location and buried him to mid thigh. The two snowmobilers then proceeded down the avalanche path, which was between 400 and 500 vertical feet. There were no injuries.  The exact time of the avalanche is unknown.

A skier triggered a slab avalanche in Picayne Gulch about 9 miles northeast of Silverton.  The skier was 10-15 feet below the fracture line when the avalanche started.  The skier was carried about 150 yards and was buried to his neck.  Two other skiers descended the slope and extricated the victim within about 10 minutes.  The avalanche also ran across San Juan County Road 2 at the base of the slope.  No injuries were reported.

Two snowmobilers were riding in an area about a half mile west of Rabbit Ears Pass.  One of the snowmobilers went up an untracked slope to make the first highmark.  The second snowmobiler started up shortly thereafter and got stuck before the first snowmobiler was off the slope. The first snowmobiler then turned and was sidehilling over to the second snowmobiler's location when the avalanche released. The avalanche caught and partially buried the second snowmobiler.  No injuries or damage were reported.

events.event_narrative: Two skiers climbed up the east face of Castle Peak during the late morning hours of the 24th. After performing several snow stability tests, the skiers saw no potential avalanche risk. Skier one was the first to descend the mountain when a slab released above him and carried him downhill. He was just coming to a stopping point when another slab released and hit him in the back, which propelled him even further downhill. The skier was carried about 750 feet, but managed to stay upright and on top of the snow surface. The skier was buried up to his boots but managed to ski out with only a minor leg injury.

Stollsteimer Creek ran out of its banks in some places within the Aspen Springs subdivision west of Pagosa Springs, which inundated some foot bridges and flooded a trailer that was flooded.  A portion of County Road 359 was also washed out due to flowing water exceeding the capacity of a 4 foot diameter culvert underneath the road. Additionally, the Navajo River also flowed out of its banks near the confluence of the Navajo and San Juan Rivers along County Road 551.

events.event_narrative: Around 2:30 pm on the afternoon of Saturday, May 22, a downed power line sparked a wildfire near the border of San Miguel and Montrose Counties along Good Enough Road. The fire spread rapidly with dry conditions and very strong southwest winds in place. Highway 145 was closed for a portion of time on Saturday due to the fire, and portions of the San Miguel River were also closed due to hazardous trees in the area. The fire continued for several days and eventually burned through roughly 2,500 acres of the Uncompahgre National Forest and nearly 430 acres of BLM land. There were no injuries or damages reported, but the estimated cost of the fire is $1,500,000. The fire continued into the month of June, so please see the June 2010 Storm Data Publication for additional information.

Heavy rainfall near Norwood caused mudslides to rush over Highway 145 between Norwood and Placerville. A storm spotter in Norwood measured 0.75 of an inch of rain within 15 minutes.  Highway 145 was closed for a period of time due to the debris on the road.

Heavy rain caused flash flooding to occur near Goulding's Lodge in the Monument Valley area of southeast Utah. Rushing water up to a foot deep flowed across County Road 420, which was washed out in one location.

A normally dry wash behind the Arches National Park Visitor Center quickly filled with runoff from heavy rain and was running 4 to 5 feet deep and 4 to 5 feet wide. Significant amounts of runoff also flowed through Courthouse Wash just west of the visitor's center.

Heavy rainfall within a short period of time resulted in flash flooding across the heavily used Mineral Bottom Road.  Mineral Bottom Road was deeply washed out in the switchback section and an extensive amount of debris covered the road, which remained impassable as of mid September 2010.  The road washout stranded 29 people who were airlifted by helicopter.  The KGJX WSR-88D radar estimated 1.86 inches of rain within 60 minutes in the source region of the Mineral Bottom Road flash flood. The NPS' Island-In-The-Sky visitors center personnel measured 1.05 inches of rain, most of which fell within a half hour. Other locations in the area likely received flash flooding.
Heavy rain caused mud and debris up to a foot deep to flow across Highway 145 near the Norwood Hill area.

A ten foot high and 30 foot wide wall of water came roaring down normally dry Tappan Wash and went out of its banks in places, including yards of residences as well as a section of Dave Wood Road.  A person hiking up the wash narrowly escaped the wall of water by quickly climbing up the wash embankment.  Culverts and irrigation canals were clogged with debris which included logs and a large amount of personal property.  Some of the personal property items were later found downstream.  A camper trailer in a yard was knocked over and damaged by the flood waters, while a nearby trailer was picked up and carried a short distance away.

Heavy rainfall from the previous night well north of Arches National Park resulted in flash flooding in the afternoon and early evening within the Salt Wash drainage that runs though Arches National Park.  Flood waters over a foot deep were flowing over the NPS road in the vicinity of Wolfe Ranch which leads to Delicate Arch.  The road was closed to traffic for at least 7 hours.

Heavy rainfall from an area of intense thunderstorms produced flash flood waters that crossed Highway 128 at a number of locations between mile markers 8 and 14.  Debris consisting mostly of mud up to two feet deep was deposited on the Highway.

A burst of rainfall during the peak snowmelt period apparently caused a debris dam to break near the headwaters of Gore Creek.  Gore Creek suddenly rose about 3 feet and stayed within the channel except in a few areas where it spread out and approached the entry of some condominiums.  Additionally, trees up to 1.5 feet in diameter came down Gore Creek and jammed up at the bridges and culverts causing additional flooding, mostly to lawns and landscaping.  A blocked culvert resulted in water flowing up to about a foot deep over Highway 24.

Heavy rainfall resulted in the Gunnison River stage rapidly rising about 4 feet through the BLM's Gunnison Gorge Wilderness Area.  Numerous camp sites and trail heads were destroyed or covered in debris and boulders to the point that they were no longer usable.  The movement of boulders and silt significantly changed the characteristic of the Gunnison River in a number of places, such as the Miracle Mile rapids where rapids no longer exist.  Six river runners were trapped at the T-Dyke boater site during the event.  Numerous small fish were killed by the flash flood.

Strong thunderstorm outflow winds flipped over two trailers, a flat bed trailer and a utility trailer, as well as some mature pine trees in the vicinity of Stevens Field Airport near Pagosa Springs.  The AWOS at the airport measured gusts to 58 mph.  There were no known eyewitnesses to this damaging wind event since it occurred shortly after midnight.
Strong thunderstorm winds that were enhanced by gradient winds blew a construction worker off a scaffolding near Whitewater.  The strong winds also blew the unfinished house off of its foundation.

A strong eastward-moving thunderstorm cell collapsed over central Delta County and produced damaging winds across portions of eastern Delta County.  Measured wind speeds included 79 mph at a location 4 miles northwest of Hotchkiss and 90 mph at a location just under 3 miles southeast of Hotchkiss.  The damage pach extended from about 5 miles west-northwest of Hotchkiss to about 7 miles east of Hotchkiss.  The width of the damage patch extended from about 2 miles north of Hotchkiss to about just north of Crawford.  Numerous trees were downed, with some trees more than 2 feet in diameter where they were snapped off.  Many houses and other personal property were damaged, including the historic brick Hotchkiss Barn.  An airplane was torn from its moorings and flipped over at the Paonia Airport.  Power was out in many locations, though it was restored at most locations by the afternoon on the following day.

Heavy rainfall caused flash flooding in the area of Dexter Creek and Skyrocket Creek north of Ouray, as well as along Cascade Creek in Ouray.  In some sections of Dexter Creek, the flash flood waters were nearly 20 feet deep.  A section of road was washed out and the remaining buildings from the abandoned Old Maid Mine and town, built in the late 1800s, were completely obliterated with only some foundations remaining. An enormous amount of debris flowed through and collected in sections of Dexter Creek, which is the main water source for many residents in Ouray County.  In particular, log jams and boulders the size of large trucks clogged a quarter-mile section of Dexter Creek, filling the creek up to 20 feet deep from the original creek bed elevation.   Skyrocket Creek flowed up to a foot deep across Highway 550 as the highway culvert was filled beyond capacity.  A motel on the west side of the highway experienced flooding in the parking lot and to some lower level motel rooms.  Skyrocket Creek deposited about 8000 cubic yards of debris, mostly rocks and boulders, in a catch basin just above the Uncompahgre River.  About 2000 cubic yards of debris filled up a catch basin near Highway 550 just before Cascade Creek dumps into the Uncompahgre River.  The Uncompahgre River gage near Ridgway measured a stage jump of nearly 2 feet that evening due to the upstream inflow from the flooding creeks.  Radar storm total rainfall estimates over the mountains near Ouray ranged from 1.5 to 1.75 inches, most of which fell within 60 minutes.

Heavy rain fell across portions of Grand County in a short period of time, resulting in minor urban and small stream flooding.  Water up to 3 inches deep ran across Highway 191 about 15 miles northwest of Moab where Courthouse Wash runs under the road.  A rainfall total of 0.63 of an inch fell within 30 minutes in Moab.
Portions of Highway 318 were washed out by flash flood waters up to a foot deep across the road.

A flash flood came down from the north in Middle Creek, flowed through culverts under I-70, and into a developed area of Vail on its way to Gore Creek.  The normally 3 foot wide placid Middle Creek was a roaring force of water 12 feet wide and over 6 feet deep.  The interior of the Vail Public Library sustained water 2 inches deep on the carpeting, and the basements of nearby lodges and condos were also flooded.  A layer of mud and other debris covered parking areas, including the Dobson Ice Arena's parking lot.  City crews worked vigorously with heavy equipment to divert the flood waters away from other locations in Vail.
Flash flooding occurred across Highway 82, with water and debris over 6 inches deep on the road in some places.
Flash flooding resulted in water and debris 6 to 12 inches deep flowing across Highway 141 in Naturita to just west of Naturita.  Highway 141 was closed until the debris was removed from the road.

Flash flood waters and debris crossed over Highway 50, leaving over a foot deep of mud and other debris on the road after the waters receded.  Highway 50 was closed until CDOT crews were able to clear the road of debris.
A flash flood over 6 inches deep flowed across the Piceance Creek Road, aka County Road 5, and left several inches of mud on the road.

A combination of heavy rainfall and a canal breach resulted in areas of flash flooding in some northern sections of Grand Junction.  The flooded areas were bounded from east to west between 27 Road and 24 Road, and from south to north between F Road and the barren hills to the north of Grand Junction Regional Airport.  The flash flooding in the eastern part of the affected area was unrelated to the canal breach.  A road just northwest of the airport was impassable with fast moving water 2 feet deep where several cars were stopped.  A woman got out of one of the cars and slipped into the fast moving water.  She was carried about a quarter mile downstream where she was rescued.  Significant erosion occurred along many sections of paved roads and at some residences.  Some outbuildings were flooded and landscaping was heavily damaged.  Several roads were closed for up to two days as repairs were made.  Natural drainages that normally only contained water flows about a foot deep were running over 12 feet deep.

A microburst initially struck the ground about a quarter mile southwest of the Northwest Colorado Community College Campus and spread out generally to the northeast from that point.  A significant portion of a roof on North Nichols Residence Hall was lifted up and blown completely over the structure. Debris from North Nichols Residence Hall was found up to a quarter mile away on the northeast end of the campus.   A dozen mature Russian Olive trees on the campus were uprooted, and large limbs and branches were snapped off many other trees. One of the uprooted trees fell against the CNCC president���s house, causing some damage to the roof.  Other wind damage to property on the CNCC campus was observed during the NWS storm survey. Further away from the CNCC campus, additional wind damage also occurred, although it was generally a little less destructive than the CNCC damage, with estimated wind gusts ranging from 55 to 70 mph. There was an observed wind speed measurement of 54 knots (62 mph) from the AWOS at the Rangely Airport (4V0) where a section of wooden fence was blown down and a swamp cooler blown from the roof of the terminal.   Many trees within the town of Rangely were uprooted or lost large limbs or branches. A few trees were snapped off a few feet above the ground, including ash trees with trunk bases generally ranging from 6 to 10 inches in diameter.   A wood frame carport was ripped off an apartment building on East Main Street. A large trampoline in the northeast part of Rangely was blown into the air and landed about 75 yards away in a neighbor���s yard, while a 400 pound water tank was blown across a road.

Heavy runoff from record snowpack kept rivers and creeks across Unitah County running at elevated to over bankfull conditions through much of June. ||The Green River exceeded flood stage on June 1st at the Jensen river gage, briefly fell below this mark between the 2nd and the 3rd, and then returned to at least a minor flood stage through the end of the month. At it's peak, the Green River at Jensen rose to a moderate flood stage level from June 9th through June 20th. During these high flows, low land flooding was reported with some damage to irrigation equipment along the river banks. Oil and gas drilling had to be halted along the river due to the impact of the high water levels. Utah Highway 88 and Chipeta Grove Road was closed for over 2 weeks near Ouray. Up to a foot of water over Highway 88 was reported with 3 to 5 feet of water inundating Chipeta Creek Road. One residence near Ouray had to be evacuated due to encroaching flood water and another house had restricted access by the flood waters. One death was attributed to the increased flows when a kayak overturned and the kayaker could not be rescued.    ||As temperatures continued to climb so did area rivers draining from the Eastern Uinta Mountains. Areal advisories and warnings were issued for much of the month of June for the Duchesne, White, White Rocks and Uinta rivers. These statements also covered may local creeks and streams that were out of their banks. The largest impact was to agricultural interests near these waterways with lowland pasture, farmland and isolated structures becoming inundated with water. Livestock and equipment had to be moved away from the flooded areas. A drinking water line that supplies areas of Unitah County had to be repaired from high water damage along the Duchesne River. Several mitigation projects needed to be done along the Uinta and White Rocks rivers and water crossed many secondary roads along the Unita River.

Many area waterways in Western Colorado, including the Colorado River, were running at or near bank full conditions to begin June as runoff was enhanced by warming temperatures over a record snow pack. Flood advisories for the Colorado River were in place all of June across Mesa County from near De Beque to the Utah state line. Flood warnings were first issued near Cameo on June 5th, and except for a brief lowering below the flood stagt from the 19th to the 23rd, the warning stayed in place through the end of the month. Minor flooding and bank erosion were experienced from De Beque to the confluence with the Gunnison River in Grand Junction. Some city recreational trails along the river washed away. Within River Bend State Park near Palisade a service road eroded away and part of the disk golf course was washed away. In some areas up to 20 feet of bank was lost to the river and a few homes in Grand Junction and Palisade reported water in the basement from the high water table. ||The Colorado River, from the confluence with the Gunnison River in Grand Junction to the Utah State line was in flood stage from June 7th to June 11th, peaking on the 8th.  In numerous places the river flooded low lying areas and approached Interstate 70. The water came within a few inches of closing the I-70 bridge near Skippers Island. A few sections of the river between Fruita and Loma lost between 20 to 30 feet of bank and some utilities were washed out. Multiple agencies and businesses worked to mitigate the flooding problems.

The Colorado River experienced elevated flows due to snow melt runoff from June 5th to the end of the month. Flood advisories or warnings were in effect through most of this time, with a few brief exceptions when the river fell just below bankfull. The main area of concern was from the confluence with the Eagle River near Dotsero to the County line just above Glenwood Canyon. Water quickly rose on the evening of June 6th when flood warnings were issued and remained in place through June 10th. Highway 6 at Dotsero was closed due to the high water levels reaching the bottom of the bridge.  The river continued to reach or exceed bankfull conditions through the end of the month, except the period of June 19th through the 24th when cooler weather reduced the heavy runoff. Lowland flooding was reported through the month and some sandbagging of residential areas were required from near Gypsum to Dotsero.

The Colorado River experienced elevated flows due to snow melt runoff from June 5th to the end of the month. Flood advisories or warnings were in effect through most of this time, with only brief periods when the river fell just below bankfull. Much of the area along the Colorado River from near the entrance to Glenwood Canyon to Rifle in Garfield County was impacted by the high flows in June. In Glenwood Canyon the water rose to within a few inches of the railroad line, inundated equipment near the river at Bair Ranch and closed the rest area along I-70 adjacent to the ranch. Portions of a recreational bike path along the river bank were under 4 to 5 feet of water and several sections were destroyed or washed downstream and cost 1.5 million dollars to repair. Low land flooding was common as the river spread hundreds of yards past the bank in several areas. Water moved into the rest area at Rifle and forced a daylong closure. During peak rises, water also inundated rail bridges leading into Rifle and flooded a Frisbee golf course in Rifle. Other flooding along the Beaver and Rifle Creek waterways caused road damage and travel inconveniences. High flows along Elk Creek caused enough bank erosion to wash away a cabin along the stream on June 13th.

Rapid snowmelt led to increased rises on area waterways across Moffat County through early June with areal flood warnings or advisories first issued on June 4th and persisting through June 22nd. The Yampa, Green and Little Snake River basins were impacted by flood waters which inundated many low lying areas. Camp site closures and bank erosions were reported along areas of the Green River in the western portions of the county. The Yampa River inundated portions of the infrastructure at Deerlodge Park in Dinosaur National Monument. Also along the Yampa River, pasture and ranch land were underwater near Craig with many outbuildings and some farm equipment being impacted. Bank erosion was also reported along both the Yampa and Little Snake Rivers due to the elevated flows.

Area creeks across Pitkin County responded to rapid snowmelt and ran at elevated levels through much of June. Areas adjacent to the Crystal river were impacted through the middle part of the month when flood advisories were in effect for near bankfull conditions. The river also briefly spiked above flood stage on June 6th near Redstone. Low land flooding was reported along the Crystal river with water and debris reaching the bottom of several bridges between Restone and Carbondale.

At the beginning of June, high flows were already occurring and a flood advisories had already been issued for the Colorado River in Grand County. These advisories remained posted throughout the month due to near bankfull conditions, though a flood warning was briefly issued from June 7th to the 11th when the gauge near the Colorado state line went above the minor flood mark. Low land flooding was the main impact along the river from the Utah state line through Westwater Canyon and back into the Moab area. Several campgrounds and a bike path were closed along Highway 128 due to flood water inundation.  Minor flooding also occurred on private property along the Colorado River in Moab. The Green River rose to near bankfull conditions around June 6th but rose out of its banks to flood level on June 9th where it remained through the end of the month. The Green River crested around 16.5 feet between June 13th and 14th. Mitigation and reinforcement work was needed along levees in and near the Green River, including work to keep water from backing up into the downtown area of the town of Green River. Sand bagging and pumping of water along the golf course and a state park were necessary to keep flood waters at bay. The Green River eventually crossed an oxbow and into crop and ranch land, though mitigation work prevented many farms and ranches along the river from being flooded.

Rapid snow melt from a record snow pack over the Northern Colorado mountains allowed many waterways across Routt County to experience increased flows through the entire month of June. Areal flood advisories and warnings were in place to cover numerous small creeks and rivers that met or exceeded bankfull conditions. Flood advisories and warnings were also issued for site specific portions of the Elk River  through the the month with the highest flows during the first half of the month and a second peak during the last few days of the month which continued into July. Preliminary data form the USGS shows historical volume and peak flow records were surpassed on this river near Milner. Significant low land flooding was reported across Routt County with some businesses and residences requiring sand bags to keep out flood waters. In rural areas, equipment and animals had to be evacuated by the encroaching water. Many local roads were also impacted with 6 to 12 inches of water being reported over the roadways.

The main stem of the Green River remained under flood conditions through July 4th, followed by lowering water levels through July 13th and included the stretch of the river from the confluence with the Yampa to near Ouray, Utah. The main impacts to the high flow was to agricultural interests due to damage of irrigation equipment and the inundation of ranch and pasture land. Oil and gas drilling operations were also negatively impacted by the high flows through early July. Smaller rivers and creeks continued to run above bankfull conditions through around July 9th, though the addition of rainfall in the middle of the month kept these waterways running high through late July. Again, the main impact was to pasture and ranch land near these rivers.

Areal flood warnings remained in effect for the first week of July along the Green River in Western Grand County, including the town of Green River. The flood stage at Green River was topped on July 2nd, where it remained for the next 5 days before slowly falling and eventually went below bank level by July 15th. Mitigation work by Grand County was needed through the first week of July to keep water off the city golf course and adjacent state park. Erosion of river banks continued during the high flows and flood waters remained over low lying ranch and farm lands near the river.

Flood warnings were in effect for the main stem Colorado River from near DeBeque to Grand Junction on the 1st of July when the river peaked at 13.41 feet. The river then began a slow descent through the remainder of the month, though it fluctuated to advisory levels through July 11th. Minor flooding and bank erosion along the river from DeBeque to the Colorado-Utah state line continued through the first part of the month due to the fast flows and near bankfull conditions.

The Elk River dropped below flood stage near Milner on July 1st and the warning was replaced with an areal flood advisoriy to cover this river and other small creeks and streams in northern Routt County. This advisory remained in place through July 10th as the river fluctuated near the flood stage through this time, then began a slow decline through the rest of the month. The river inundated farm and ranch land and the flood waters also encroached on a few residences. Several local and rural roadways were also under water through the first week of July.

High releases were necessary to alleviate inflated inflow into Flaming Gorge Reservoir due to heavy runoff from melting snow that occurred from the record snow pack in the Central Rockies. The high releases created low land flooding below the reservoir, caused some bank erosion and impacted recreation along the river.

events.cz_name: GORE AND ELK MOUNTAINS/CENTRAL MOUNTAIN VALLEYS
events.event_narrative: A small avalanche was triggered in a nnarrow gully by a skier. A second skier become stuck in the initial avalanche debris field and triggered another avalanche when trying to extricate himself. This skier was then buried by the second avalanche in a terrain trap where he was buried for approximately 10 minutes before being uncovered by other skiers.  This fatal avalanche occurred in the Burnt Mountain area outside the boundaries of Snowmass Ski Area.

events.cz_name: GORE AND ELK MOUNTAINS/CENTRAL MOUNTAIN VALLEYS
events.event_narrative: Five skiers entered the Prima Cornice area inside the Vail Ski Area boundary where unstable snow conditions were in place. Three of the skiers traversed a slope and were caught in a 200 foot-wide soft-slab avalanche which began at the 10,800 foot level and ran 400 vertical feet through a forested area on a 46 degree slope.  Two skiers were partially buried and another tumbled outside of the debris field. One of the partially buried skiers died from injuries sustained in the avalanche.

A snowboarder traveling alone was caught in an avalanche which initiated at the 10,300 foot level and carried the victim downhill 925 vertical feet.  The victim had an avalanche beacon and was found buried under four feet of snow and debris. The avalanche occurred in an area south of the town of Telluride.

Heavy snowfall in favorable terrain caused several small avalanches along the Highway 550 corridor near Red Mountain Pass. Avalanche debris depth on the highway was up to six feet deep.  The highway was closed until the debris was removed, and it was closed again later that day for several hours to do avalanche mitigation work.

A skier in a group of four decided to ski down a southeast aspect near Ophir Pass during a sunny and relatively warm afternoon. This skier initiated a wet slab avalanche that broke loose at about the 12,800 foot level and traveled a distance of over one mile with a path width of up to 500 feet. The skier was carried by the avalanche a total distance of about 4200 feet down a vertical elevation drop of about 1500 feet. Although the skier had an avalanche beacon, he was not found and uncovered from the avalanche debris until about 35 minutes after he was buried.

A group of four snowmobile riders were heading into the Beaver Basin area and noticed the snow pack becoming increasingly unstable by the late morning hours. The group found a turn-around point in a nearby meadow which was in the avalanche zone. The last rider heading to the meadow turn-around point was caught by a massive avalanche which released higher up on the mountain.  The victim and his snowmobile were buried under about twelve feet of snow, and were not able to be extricated until the next day.  The top of the avalanche path was near the 11,200 foot level and traveled down about 1250 vertical feet with a path width of up to 800 feet.

events.cz_name: GORE AND ELK MOUNTAINS/CENTRAL MOUNTAIN VALLEYS
events.event_narrative: A trio of skiers entered Mushroom Bowl near Vail Ski Area.  One skier jumped off a 30 foot cliff onto the snow below and triggered an avalanche which started at the 11,450 foot level.  The avalanche path was 100 feet wide and 300 vertical feet. The skier who initiated the avalanche was swept off his feet and carried into a group of small trees, where he received non-life threatening injuries, then became fully buried under one to two feet of snow from a secondary avalanche. The other skiers where able to dig him out then self evacuate from the avalanche site.

A large group of skiers were touring the backcountry near Red Mountain pass when one skier triggered an avalanche at the 10,520 foot level. This skier was not caught by the avalanche but two others were caught and buried by the avalanche which deposited avalanche debris up to ten feet deep along the creek bottom. Both skiers where located within 5 minutes, with one buried two feet beneath the snow and the other buried six feet under the snow.  Both skiers survived without injuries.

The Pine Ridge fire was started by lightning June 27th and continued to burn until fully contained on the afternoon of July 4th. The fire threatened numerous resource concerns, such as oil and gas well locations, cultural resources, threatened and endangered species, and the Wild Horse range. However, the only losses were to three unoccupied tents and two camper units. The fire was halted within a mile of a farm residence near De Beque. Interstate 70 and the local rail line were temporarily closed during the height of fire activity in late June.

A skier triggered an avalanche which swept him down approximately 50 vertical feet and partially buried him under 12 to 18 inches of debris. The skier was conscious and breathing when uncovered by fellow riders approximately 3 minutes after the avalanche.  There were no reported injuries.

A party of three skiers triggered an avalanche in the Cement Creek drainage area of the northwest San Juan Mountains. The slide occurred on a steep northeast aspect known as Clothesline Path. The steepness of this slope, combined with new snowfall over a weakened slab of older snow, created dangerous avalanche conditions. Two of the skiers were partially buried with non-critical injuries, while the third skier was fully buried and did not survive after being uncovered several minutes after the avalanche.

The last in a group of 4 skiers triggered a shallow avalanche along a slope favorable for releases due to a weakened snow pack. This shallow slide triggered a larger avalanche that broke to the surface. This larger avalanche carried the skier approximately 250 vertical feet down to the valley floor where he was fully buried. The remaining skiers performed search and rescue operations and found the buried skier about 10 minutes after the avalanche. The skier was unable to be revived.

events.cz_name: GORE AND ELK MOUNTAINS/CENTRAL MOUNTAIN VALLEYS
events.event_narrative: This hard slab avalanche released on a north facing slope at the 11,900 foot level and ran almost a half mile of distance, and 900 vertical feet.  The crown face of the avalanche was 850 feet wide and was up to 12 feet deep. The debris path covered about 10 acres.  Two snowboarders were caught in the avalanche, with one having triggered the avalanche.  The snowboarder who triggered the avalanche was not buried but was carried through an area of trees and the resultant injuries were fatal.  The other snowboarder was carried by the avalanche off to the side of the slide path and was uninjured.

Heavy rainfall resulted in flash flooding within various locations in and near Pagosa Springs.  Flowing water about 18 inches deep ran across Highway 160 about a half mile east of the junction with Highway 84.  A stream which comes down to Rumbaugh Road in northeast Pagosa Springs had a high volume of water which ran across the road and continued onto Highway 160; with water 6 to 8 inches deep in an area generally bounded on the east and west ends by 1st Street and 2nd Street and bounded on the north and south ends by Lewis Street and Highway 160. Water damage occurred to a number of residences and businesses, including an auto supply store which still had about 12 inches of standing water inside the store the next morning.  The river gauge in the San Juan River within Pagosa Springs measured a stage rise of just over 3 feet in less than 1.5 hours.
